#6512. The 15 Best Appetizers at Trader Joe’s

Why is Trader Joe’s so good at making small foods? I’m thinking it’s Newton’s Third Law, providing balance to all of Costco’s extra-large foods. Remind me to bring this up at my next dinner party when I pull a batch of Parmesan Pastry Pups out of the air fryer to serve to my guests. If you’ve been a long-time shopper at Trader Joe’s, you know that this grocery store does frozen appetizers better than actual dinners. So if you’re preparing for marathon holiday hosting, here’s my list of the best bite-size apps, in order from the least messy to most messy. They can almost all be prepared in the air fryer too, which frees up your larger oven for the enchiladas I hope are for dinner. Always hoping.

Adorable little tarts! These are what I like to snatch at a wedding cocktail reception the second the servers glide through the saloon doors. Savory mushrooms, buttery pie crust. For a faux-made flourish, buy a package of chives to slice and sprinkle over.

Mess-o-meter: 1/10. You can pop the whole tartelette in your mouth and forget it ever even happened.

Love this new addition. You can fry them up before guests arrive because they’re very very hot right out of the pan and the rice paper wrappers stay nicely crisp. My only gripe is these don’t come with a dipping sauce, so pick up a bag of scallions to slice and scatter over—nice touch—and the Gyoza Dipping Sauce. Or make your own with soy sauce, rice vinegar, and sugar.

Mess-o-meter: 1/10. These are also a one-to-two-bite chopstick situation with a well-contained filling.

An absolute icon in the Trader Joe’s frozen aisle. These fried mac and cheese balls are arancini’s Gen Z cousin, replacing its job at a quarter of the price (the price of cooking prep time, in this case). Adorable, delicious, crunchy, oozy. If these are at your party, served with a pepper jelly or spicy mayo getup, I won’t sneak out the backdoor like I usually do.

Mess-o-meter: 2/10. You’ll need a cocktail napkin or little plate to help contain the ooze. Dip in marinara (fun) and it escalates to a 3.

You really want crab rangoons, but your guests will still be thrilled with this riff, which has a wee bit of jalapeño, not enough to shoot steam from your ear canals. Make sure to pick up a dipping sauce—Pepper Jelly, always, or Sweet Chili Sauce. Sometimes these can come out a little dry on the exterior, especially if you air-fry them. Try tossing (or spraying) them in oil for a crispier, browner exterior.

Mess-o-meter: 2/10. Someone will probably drip dipping sauce on the tablecloth.

Another classic party food. These two-bite samosas have approx one Lego cube of potato, a single pea, and maybe a flake of cilantro inside, but they’re the perfect beer snack. For dunking, the Sri Lankan Mango Chutney would be nice here.

Mess-o-meter: 2/10. While the crust is nice and crisp, it stays pretty contained when you bite in.

Trader Joe’s dips are hit or miss—this one’s a hit. Not exactly queso like my mama made, but after a few tequilas no one seems to care. It’s thick molten cheese with a gentle kick. The key is to transfer it to a cute bowl, microwave it, and hide the original packaging deep in the recycling. I like Trader Joe’s Restaurant Style Tortilla Chips, which are sturdy and very salty, but others prefer the classic rounds or the moody blue corn ones. Your choice.

Mess-o-meter: 3/10. Impatient dippers will leave a trail of queso, these are facts of life.

Make a version of one of Bon Appétit’s swankiest yet simplest party tricks—marinated salami and almonds—with Trader Joe’s standbys. The rosemary-flavored Marcona almonds are buttery and crunchy. I don’t love the salami at Trader Joe’s, but the secret to this “recipe” is that the oil, lemon, and pepper make even the cheap stuff taste gourmet.

Mess-o-meter: 3/10. Oily! You’ll need a napkin or hunks of baguette to catch those drips.

I’ve been eating these French-accented ham pizzas (tartes, sure) as long as I’ve been shopping at Trader Joe’s, which is…20 years now. The crust is paper thin, the Gruyère is generously laden, and it cooks in under 15 minutes. If you’re sharing with guests, cut it into small rectangles to avoid floppy slices. (Or save the floppies for yourself.)

Mess-o-meter: 3/10. The toppings can be gooey and may overfloweth.

No cooking, just light assembly. Trader Joe’s recently added mortadella is great for draping directly into the mouth, but for an entertaining scenario, you can make these “mortadella moments” which are classy sliders. Trader Joe’s focaccia, sliced and toasted, will do the trick, or their ciabatta, sliced into small squares.

Mess-o-meter: 4/10. Bread crumbs happen. Perhaps a pickle makes a run for it.

These baby shrimp bao need to be eaten pretty soon after steaming (or microwaving), so they’re great for, like, a Gilded Age viewing party where your guests are glued to the couch, waiting for you to bring them fresh snacks like the good servant you are. The buns are soft and spongy, the shrimp patties decently seasoned, and they’re easy to improve with carrots, cukes, and scallions. Plus, unlike a lot of TJ apps, they come with a lip-smacky lemongrass dipping sauce.

Mess-o-meter: 4/10. These are pretty tidy but your added garnishes may fling about.

Keep it simple. Sometimes the best appetizer isn’t an air-fried novelty, but a nice cheese you’ve let come to room temperature—30 minutes, please—a salty cracker, and a pinch pot o’ jelly. Old Amsterdam is always in stores and the ultimate crowdpleaser, but go for goat cheese or blue cheese or even feta if you’re feeling festive. I’ve got other favorite Trader Joe’s cheeses here.

Mess-o-meter: 4/10. Expect typical cheese board detritus, like the tragic hollowed-out cheese rind.

Hello, these are mini Bloomin’ Onions! There are only two “flowers” to a box, so these are an appetizer for a more intimate occasion, unless you’re feeling ambitious and spendy. Invite me if you are. Make sure to cook until nicely golden brown and to pick up a bottle of Buttermilk Ranch (near the bagged salads) to accompany.

Mess-o-meter: 8/10. You will tear into these with your rabid paws, so fried onion petals will leave crumbs and oop, ya need to wipe your face a little there.

These are fried, tangled veggie tempura fritters that guests can pop into their mouths while leaving greasy fingerprints on your furniture. The soy dipping sauce could use a few fresh scallions or chives, but you can do that. These have been at Trader Joe’s for decades; they’re a classic for a reason.

Mess-o-meter: 8/10. It’s a fritter with crispy bits and pieces, but that’s why we love ’em.

Welcome to the flaky pastry portion of our evening. You might know these pups as “pigs in a blanket” but Joe has never been one to follow convention. (Just profits lol.) Pair with Hot Honey Mustard and always buy one more box than you think is needed.

Mess-o-meter: 9/10. Think of puff pastry’s flaky confetti as spontaneous party decor. It means your guests are having a good time, all over your rug.

For a homemade-ish appetizer, I like to do these easy puff pastry cheese twists from Dessert Person Claire Saffitz. The twists look nice but when you don’t have time for arts and crafts, I have a shortcut: Defrost puff pastry. Roll it out a smidge. Brush with egg wash. Sprinkle with cheese and spices. Bake at 400° until browned. Cut into squares. Bask in the glory.

Mess-o-meter: 10/10. This is a beautiful mess. But don’t worry about it. You’ll vacuum tomorrow.

#6511. Starbucks Just Revealed Its 2026 Holiday Cups—And There's An Unexpected Addition This Year

There's a lot more to the designs than Christmas trees and bows.

It's already November, and I'm still trying to accept that I'll be leaving the house in the dark for the next several months. But at least there are festive drinks to warm us up, plenty of Christmas songs to listen to, and one annual tradition that makes the changing seasons a little easier to accept.

Starbucks' 2026 holiday cup collection has officially arrived, and this year's designs look like something you'd find among the Christmas decorations your family has been hanging up for decades. You’ll find four versions for hot drinks, adorned with trees, bows, and stars, with the usual red and green joined by shades of mint, cream, cranberry, and gold.

And for anyone who refuses to stop ordering iced coffee just because it's freezing outside (read: me), there's a cold version covered in greenery and red bows.

According to the coffee giant, Starbucks started thinking about these designs nearly two years ago. London D., who oversaw the creative work, told the company that one of the team's early inspirations was “real physical ribbons.” The idea eventually went beyond the cups, showing up on other packaging and even in the decorations inside Starbucks stores.

There's another addition this year, although the intended customers probably won't appreciate the artwork quite as much. For the first time, Starbucks has made a 3.5-ounce holiday pup cup, featuring an illustration of Junie, a real-life beagle. Personally, I don't think dogs care much about what their whipped cream is served in, but it's a cute touch nonetheless.

Red Cup Day is also returning on November 17, which gives a free reusable red cup to anyone who purchases a handcrafted holiday beverage at a participating Starbucks, while they have ‘em in stock.

As for the more permanent additions, Starbucks has a Christmas tree-shaped glass cold cup ($32.95), a Bearista ornament ($16.95), and a stainless-steel Bearista tumbler ($29.95) among its new merchandise. And after the madness surrounding the original Bearista glass, the company is releasing mystery-box versions on November 10, followed by another round of the original on December 1.

Say what you want about Starbucks, but they certainly know how to do the holidays right.

#6509. Spinach Artichoke Baked Potatoes

This baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s important that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

While potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

Mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

#6508. Burger King's New Advent Calendar Has A Big Surprise Behind Its 12 Doors

Last year's disappeared in minutes. Consider yourself warned.

Remember when Advent calendars were just little cardboard boxes with a piece of chocolate behind each door? Nowadays, you can find them filled with everything from beauty products to booze—and apparently, miniature fast food restaurants.

Burger King's Advent calendar is returning for a third year, and this time, you can practically open your own franchise.

If you remember last year's edition, it was packed with some pretty unexpected throwbacks, including Cini Mini-inspired candles, a tiny board game, and a JD the Dog plush. Fans ate it up, too, as Burger King said its last two calendars sold out in less than five minutes.

For 2026, the chain has ditched the assortment of random collectibles for something you can actually put together. Joel Yashinsky, Burger King's chief marketing officer, said fans can “build their very own BK restaurant.”

Behind the 12 doors are miniature versions of just about everything you'd find at your local BK: There's a Whopper with its own box, fries, nuggets, a soda fountain, a booth, employees, and customers. And of course, who can forget the essential Christmas tree and a reindeer pairing, too.

The only thing missing is food you can actually eat, although the final compartment does include a $5 digital offer for eligible Royal Perks members.

Now, if you want to get your hands on one, you'll have five chances. Burger King is releasing just 110 calendars each day from November 16 through November 20, with sales starting at 12 p.m. ET exclusively at BKAdventCalendar.com.

Each costs $19.54, a reference to the year Burger King was founded, and orders are limited to one per household, with free standard shipping to the contiguous U.S. and Washington, D.C. If you manage to snag one of the Advent calendars, expect it to ship the week of November 30.

So have yourself a merry little Whopper this Christmas. And I do mean little.

An American astronaut on board the ISS recently snapped a spectacular "fireball" streaking across the nighttime sky over West Africa. The striking "light show" shows a Russian rocket being vaporized as it reenters the upper atmosphere.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What's in the photos? Space debris from a Russian rocket burning up upon reentry

Who took the photos? NASA astronaut Chris Williams

Earlier this year, an astronaut on board the International Space Station (ISS) snapped some striking photos, and an eerily beautiful video, of a "fireball" streaking over Earth as chunks of space debris burned up in the nighttime sky.

NASA's Chris Williams, who lived and worked on the ISS between November 2025 and July 2026, captured the eye-catching images from the station's cupola — a large, roughly dome-shaped series of windows that constantly points down at our planet — and later shared them on the social media platform X.

"Just as we were passing over West Africa, I saw a bright object directly below us, streaking through the upper atmosphere," Williams wrote in the post. "I saw its tail grow and then split apart into a shower of smaller pieces," he added. "It was quite a light show!"

Williams initially peered down at Earth to catch a glimpse of the Russian cargo spacecraft Progress 95, which successfully delivered essential supplies and additional equipment to the ISS later the same day. Instead, he saw what he believed was "some piece of orbital debris or a satellite breaking up as it entered the atmosphere."

Live Science's sister site Space.com later revealed that Williams had actually witnessed the burning remains of the Russian Soyuz rocket that had carried Progress 95 into space, after it lifted off from a recently repaired launchpad at the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.

The Soyuz rocket launched the cargo spacecraft Progress 95, which later docked with the ISS. (This photo shows the Progress 46 mission docking with the station in 2011.)

Shortly after deploying the resupply shuttle into low Earth orbit, the rocket's fairings and booster fell back toward our planet as expected, breaking apart into smaller pieces that were superheated and later vaporized by intense friction as they hit the upper atmosphere, according to Space.com. A very similar fireball was seen above Australia in August 2023, when another Soyuz rocket reentered the atmosphere.

Russia's prior resupply mission, Progress 94, also made headlines earlier this year when one of its antennae failed to deploy after separation from its Soyuz rocket, forcing cosmonauts (Russian astronauts) to use a remote control "backup system" to dock the spacecraft to the ISS.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Historically, the only fireballs visible in Earth's skies have been those caused by meteors, which can similarly break apart in flames. We were recently reminded of this when fireballs were spotted above the U.S. this spring, including one space rock that exploded with a massive sonic boom over Ohio and another that crashed through the roof of a house in Houston. (A NASA statement said the fireball Williams witnessed also may have been caused by meteor activity but was more likely to be the Soyuz rocket.)

However, fireballs from human-made objects are becoming more common. The number of spacecraft orbiting Earth has skyrocketed (pun intended) in recent decades, and "what goes up must come down."

Williams' photographs show how the remains of the Soyuz rocket exploded in a bright flash before stretching out into a train of flaming debris.

Most spacecraft and large pieces of space junk burn up around 50 miles (80 kilometers) above Earth's surface — just below the imaginary boundary with space, known as the Kármán line. While this may lead to visually stunning spectacles like the one Williams captured, scientists are starting to realize that these fireballs may be having a bigger impact on the upper atmosphere than they previously expected.

In recent years, researchers have detected a sharp increase in atmospheric metal pollution from vaporized spacecraft. And while they are still trying to figure out what effect this may have, some scientists have proposed that it could affect the ozone layer or potentially alter Earth's magnetic field.

Additionally, as the number of falling spacecraft rises, the chances that debris may fall to Earth's surface — after failing to properly burn up upon reentry — also increase. This came to the fore in March 2024, when the remains of a 3-ton battery pack that was discarded from the ISS crashed into a family home in Florida.

This 2011 astronaut photo captured one of NASA's iconic space shuttles passing between Earth and the International Space Station for the very last time.

During the Sept. 11 attacks, NASA astronaut Frank Culbertson — the only American not on Earth at the time — snapped a "sobering" shot of smoke pouring across New York City as the second tower fell.

A 2016 satellite photo shows Hurricane Madeline and Hurricane Lester heading straight toward Hawaii. When viewed from above, the twin cyclones and the surrounding clouds look eerily like a giant smiley face.

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. #6505. How a Jungle Farm in the Yucatán Is Transforming Its Maya Community

“The future is ancestral,” said Gonzalo Samaranch Granados. “Mayans were very good observers of the sky, but also the jungle and its complex relationship of plants and animals.” The rainy season, when farming deep in the Yucatán jungle proves more challenging than usual, had ended, and he was preparing for the next growing cycle, when the garden beds at Mestiza de Indias, a 550-acre reserve and biodiversity lab, would once again sprout heirloom tomatoes, eggplant, carrots, kale, garlic, herbs—crops popular with restaurant and chef collaborators on the Riviera Maya—as well as indigenous varieties with deep cultural significance for the local Mayan community.

Mak’ulan (pepperleaf), pepitas, and maize form the base of the kots’ob tamales prepared by market stall women in the nearby town of Espita. Cempasúchil (marigolds) decorate altars during Día de Muertos. Tomatillos milperos (purple tomatillos) introduced from Hidalgo are added to sikil p’aak and sopa de lima. Samaranch selects and saves native seeds, but he also sources from organic seed companies such as Baker’s Creek and Kitazawa. He’s currently on the hunt for wild ts’unu’un p’aak, or hummingbird tomatoes, a variety endemic to the Yucatán.

Other passion projects at Mestiza de Indias include the cultivation of rare Maya vanilla orchids and the extraction of a citrusy honey produced by endangered Melipona bees. (Ancient Mayans were avid apiarists. Ah Muzen Kab, the Maya god of bees, is featured in the 1,100-year-old Madrid Codex, which also contains detailed instructions for beekeeping.) Next to a ts’iits’il che’ tree where orchid vines twined, Samaranch walked into a screened enclosure protecting square wood boxes that serve as hives for these stingless bees. He removed the top of one to reveal treasure: Instead of combs, the bees create waxen pods, oozing amber-hued honey. It’s never a lot, so every precious taste is bittersweet. Equally important, they are critical pollinators for tropical ecosystems and go crazy for the nectar of ts’iits’il che’ blossoms, which flower after the first rainfall after the dry season. “What we do is possible because I was fascinated by traditional Mayan agriculture,” said Samaranch, a native of Barcelona who traded the art world for regenerative farming. “It’s not only making food. This system is related to culture, medicine, spirituality. It’s about living in harmony with nature, a respectful system.”

This Mesoamerican worldview is known as the milpa. In the Yucatán, it refers to the symbiotic planting of corn, beans, and squashes, often called the Three Sisters, on small-acre farms. (Other Indigenous growers consider sunflowers or bee balm the fourth sister. And when watermelon was introduced to the New World in the 16th century, it was adopted as a sister, too.) The concept of caring for the land, putting back more than you take, replenishing waterways, and reviving heritage crops manifests differently across continents and climates, but it exists wherever farming communities still observe old and slow ways.

By adapting these polyculture techniques into a regenerative project, Samaranch is transforming both the land and its people, including the way they look at the culture of food itself. And he’s not alone: In Australia’s Far East Gippsland, Bruce Pascoe founded Black Duck Foods to perpetuate Aboriginal land-management traditions. Black Duck: A Year at Yumburra is his manifesto about caring for country but also a personal reclamation after devastating bushfires and the loss of elders.At Royal Queen Farms in Acadia Parish, Louisiana, artist and land steward Michelle Joan Papillion has created a food sovereignty network for her community while protecting species native to the region. Johnny Ortiz-Concha and his wife, Maida Branch, bring people together around a communal table at /shed, a subscription supper club that consciously celebrates their ancestry and ecosystem. Menus are based on the crops and livestock they raise or forage at their ranch outside Taos Pueblo. They are custodians of a landrace variety of blue corn known as Tu-ah-tah, gifted to the couple by Ortiz-Concha’s family.

For those who work at Mestiza des Indias, change also starts close to home. The reserve lies almost four miles down a rough track outside the Mayan village of San Pedro Chenchelá, where most residents still live in primitive casa de huano, or mud-daubed wooden houses thatched with palm, and wear brightly patterned huipils, the distinctive Mayan tunic that predates Hispanic fashions. Hiking on foot to the milpa, field-workers have to beware of jaguars, rattlesnakes, and even poisonous trees.

During high season, Samaranch presently employs about 10 workers, most of them women whose husbands commute to the coast for tourism-related jobs. Others leave for bigger cities. Because family members can be away from home for extended periods, this has disrupted the ancestral rhythm of life. And when they do return to the community, it’s often with addiction problems. Even deep in the Yucatán jungle, the arrival of methamphetamine has devastated the region’s younger generation.

To counter this cultural disruption, Samaranch’s Mayan wife, Martha Elena Chan Tuz, a community project leader and former municipal tourism secretary, launched a complementary initiative, forming a cooperative of local needlework crafters who hand embroider table linens with intricate xookbil chuy, or cross-stitches. Their exquisite dinner napkins appear on tables during a communal meal in La Ceiba Garden & Kitchen at Rosewood Mayakoba. “Bien contentas,” said Chan Tuz, when asked how her neighbors have responded to the project. Samaranch explained: “It gives the women some independence. They have money and can manage their time. It’s something positive and very helpful, a job they can combine with what they do at home. Normally, they have to ask permission to work with us, but in this case, the men are grateful the women can contribute.”

Each worker gets to take home a basket of produce from the milpa as part of their wages. With only modest tiendas that stock junk food and shelf-stable canned goods, it’s generally a struggle to put fresh, healthy food on the table. (Especially when backyard milpas go untended because breadwinners are absent.) “We thought the people who grow the food should eat the food,” said Samaranch. “They get the same as the resorts we supply, so we have changed the diet.” He explained that children in San Pedro Chenchelá and the neighboring village of Kunché are now more excited about vegetables than soda or chips. “When a kid asks, ‘When will the eggplants be ready again?’ I feel we’re doing right.”

#6503. Dunkin' Is Making 3 Childhood Cereal Favorites A Little More Grown-Up

I didn't think my childhood breakfast needed a makeover, but I'm willing to hear them out.

I'm not that convinced Cinnamon Toast Crunch, Reese's Puffs, or Golden Grahams need much improving. All three have been breakfast staples for decades, and based on how long they’ve been on store shelves, it’s clear they've done pretty well for themselves.

But if we're going to mess with the cereals we grew up eating, borrowing a few flavors from Dunkin' isn't the worst idea.

The chain is teaming up with General Mills on three limited-edition varieties arriving this December, each taking its own approach to the coffee-influenced variation.

The new Peanut Butter Mocha flavor sounds like a pretty natural fit, considering chocolate and peanut butter are already involved. Meanwhile, Cinnamon Toast Crunch Cinnamon Caramel Latte adds a little caramel to its familiar cinnamon flavor, while Golden Grahams Vanilla Graham Latte gives those honey-graham squares a vanilla coffee-shop makeover.

And before any parents start worrying about their kids bouncing off the walls after breakfast, there's no actual coffee or caffeine in these boxes. The flavors are inspired by Dunkin's drinks, so unfortunately, you'll still need the real thing if you're looking for a morning pick-me-up.

Brian Gilbert, vice president of retail business development at Inspire Brands, said in a statement that the collaboration allows Dunkin' to “bring the flavors of some fan-favorite Dunkin’ beverages beyond the cup and into the cereal bowl.”

All three are scheduled to arrive in December, although you'll have to visit Walmart specifically for the Golden Grahams version, while the other two will be available at retailers nationwide.

And judging by early reactions online, plenty of people are just as interested as I am in giving them a shot.

"Those Golden Grahams finna slap 👋🏽" one person predicted, while another wrote, "I'm definitely going try all of them 💯". General Mills' previous cereal experiments seem to have earned it some goodwill, too. Its Reese's Puffs PB&J variety got a shoutout from one fan: "The pb&j Reese's cereal is really good. Excited for these!"

And someone else decided to get to the point and address Dunkin' directly, writing, "let me go head and send you my address NOW!!!"

As someone who loves the taste of coffee, I have a feeling these are going to be right up my alley. My morning iced coffee, though? That's never getting replaced.

#6500. These Wine Glasses Are the Only Ones That Can Survive My Clumsiness

I spent years living with roommates and making due with our collective assortment of mismatched dishware, throwing washed take-out containers haphazardly into a cupboard and reusing them until they were cracked and stained, and living with a pantry that was in a constant state of moderate disarray. But when I moved in with my boyfriend, I took the opportunity to get my shit together. I pride myself on being a relatively put-together person, and that now translates to my kitchen too. I’ve got a cabinet full of well-organized food storage containers with their corresponding lids, I keep my spices neatly stacked in deli containers with labeled with color-coded kitchen tape, I replaced my chipped water glasses with a matching set, and I have a special drawer that houses the linens, taper candles, and flatware I pull out when I’m hosting. It all feels very adult.

Until recently, though, there was one remaining aspect of my kitchen that still needed help. While I have more fun coupes and rocks glasses than I know what to do with, I haven’t owned a matching set of wine glasses since college—in fact, at the time of my move, I had two left to my name. It’s not for lack of trying: I’ve tested out glassware during my time at BA, bringing home countless options in the hopes that they’d be my forever stems. I’ve somehow managed to break every single one of them, which has become a running joke for those that know me.

But despite my clumsiness, I’m not willing to sacrifice style for durability. I want a thin-stemmed, thin-rimmed, elegant wine glass that won’t snap in two the minute I lay my hands on it. Is that too much to ask?

For the longest time, I thought it might be, and had resigned myself to sipping wine out of stemless tumblers—until I discovered Gabriel-Glas’s StandArt All Purpose Wine Glass. They’ve got a sleek, slightly conical shape that I find enhances reds, whites, and rosés alike, with a slight curve between the bowl and the rim that adds a touch of personality to an otherwise classic silhouette. The stem is thin enough to satisfy my desire for elegance without being so delicate that I’m scared I’ll snap it, and the laser-cut rim is a joy to sip from.

Because the glasses are machine-blown from a single piece of molten crystal, they have none of the weak points that tend to form where traditional multipart glasses are joined. The machine-blown construction also keeps the cost per glass low enough that I won’t mind replacing one if (let’s be real, when) I do drop and shatter it. But I’m pleased to report that as of right now, all six of my beloved StandArt glasses are intact and ready to take on my new apartment’s first season of holiday hosting and cozy weather hangs. Bring on the winter reds and festive bottles of bubbly.

NASA's Swift Observatory is about to make a fiery reentry through Earth's atmosphere after a private mission to save it failed. Most of the spacecraft will burn up in orbit.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Editor's note: As of 11:15 a.m. EST on Wednesday (Nov. 4), NASA and the Aerospace Corporation both predict that the Swift observatory could have reentered Earth's atmosphere by now. However, no new details on reentry have been provided. Stay tuned for more updates about where and when the telescope will fall.NASA's decades-old Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is rapidly falling out of orbit and could tumble back to Earth any moment now, the space agency says.

According to NASA's latest estimates, shared Monday (Nov. 2), the roughly 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) spacecraft was likely to reenter Earth's atmosphere around 3:30 a.m. EST Wednesday (Nov. 4), with an uncertainty of plus or minus 11 hours — meaning the defunct observatory could have plunged down as early as Tuesday evening, and as late as Wednesday afternoon.

An independent analysis from the private nonprofit Aerospace Corporation, which tracks thousands of objects in orbit, similarly estimates that the telescope should have reentered the atmosphere at 6:56 a.m. EST Wednesday, give or take three hours. Both estimates suggest the Swift spacecraft could have already met its demise as of Wednesday morning, though no official confirmation has been shared.

As with all spacecraft reentries, the risk to humans is minimal. Most of the Swift telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere, according to NASA. Any surviving fragments will likely fall somewhere between 20.6 degrees south latitude and 20.6 degrees north latitude — a range that includes parts of Mexico, the Caribbean, Central and South America, the Arabian Peninsula, India, Africa and Oceania, but also a lot of ocean.

NASA predicts that the chances of Swift debris falling over a populated area are approximately 1 in 2,100. For comparison, the odds of a person being struck by lightning in their lifetime are 1 in 15,300, according to the National Weather Service.

NASA will continue to update their predictions as the reentry window draws closer.

Swift has detected thousands of deep-space explosions, including sudden flares from neutron stars (illustrated here).

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is a multiwavelength optical, ultraviolet and X-ray telescope that launched in November 2004 on a mission to study the most powerful explosions in space. Initially designed for a two-year primary mission, the telescope ultimately spent more than 10 times that duration hunting for supernovas, gamma-ray bursts and black-hole-induced eruptions around the universe.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Swift has been rapidly losing altitude for more than a year, after rampant solar activity increased the drag on the aging spacecraft. This past August, a costly mission to boost Swift's orbit with a private spacecraft failed shortly after launch, hammering the final nail in Swift's coffin.

Engineers on the Swift team officially shut down the observatory's science operations on Oct. 20, after the spacecraft fell too low in orbit to continue taking steady observations of the sky.

As Swift goes out with a fiery bang, it leaves behind a trove of scientific data, including contributions to more than 7,000 scientific papers so far, according to NASA. This number will only increase as Swift's final observations are processed.

#6495. Spiced and Glazed Roast Turkey

Our mission: A roast turkey that’s boldly spiced, beautifully glazed, and—can we type this loudly enough?—PROPERLY COOKED. That means juicy breast meat, tender dark meat, and plenty of deeply browned skin. Andy Baraghani and Brad Leone’s solution? Break the bird into five pieces: two wings, two legs, and one whole breast. Roasting the bird in parts gives you more control over when each piece is done—no dry breast meat or tough legs.

They didn’t slouch on flavor either. A peppery dry brine with garlic powder, onion powder, and smoked paprika gets to work 24–48 hours before the turkey goes into the oven. Then comes the glaze: a savory-tangy mix of soy sauce, vinegar, brown sugar, orange zest, and herbs. Brushed onto the turkey as it roasts, it builds a glossy, deeply burnished finish. And because the pieces cook on a wire rack set inside a baking sheet, you get more exposed skin for browning and a more even cook overall.

If the idea of doing surgery on a raw turkey gives you a stress rash, ask your butcher to do it—even at the supermarket. Request a 12–14-lb. turkey cut into five pieces, with the thighs attached to the drumsticks, the breast left whole, and the backbone removed. If they ask why, just say: Yes, you’re making that ridiculous Bon Appétit recipe. If you’d rather do the honors yourself, here’s our guide to breaking down a whole turkey.

Choose an unbrined turkey for this recipe. Many supermarket birds are already treated with a salt solution, sometimes labeled “self-basting,” “enhanced,” or “contains a solution.” Adding this dry brine on top can make the turkey overly salty. Check the packaging before you buy.

Should I rinse off the dry brine before roasting?

No. Leave the seasoning on the turkey when you coat it with oil. Some of the spice mixture may rub off, but that’s fine. There’s no need to rinse the bird, and washing raw poultry can spread bacteria around your kitchen.

Can I use the pan drippings to make gravy?

Yes, but taste them first. Between the seasoned dry brine and soy-based glaze, the drippings can be quite salty and intensely flavored. Use them sparingly and taste your gravy before adding more salt. For a simpler option, try our Make-Ahead Gravy, which doesn’t require drippings at all.

Read our guide to turkey cooking times, no matter the bird’s size or your preferred cooking method.

4 hours 45 minutes, plus at least 24 hours dry-brining

Place one 12–14-lb. turkey, neck and giblets removed, breast side up, on a cutting board and pat dry. Grip a wing and pull it outward so you can see where it attaches to the body. Using a sharp boning or chef’s knife, cut through the joint to separate the wing from the breast (if you hit bone, you’re in the wrong spot; pull the wing out farther to help you get into the place where the joint meets the socket). Remove wing; repeat on the other side.

Cut through skin connecting 1 leg to carcass. Pull leg back until the ball joint pops out of its socket; cut through the joint to separate leg. Repeat on the other side.

Now for the breast: Position the turkey breast side down with the opening facing you. Using kitchen shears, cut along one side of backbone until you get all the way through the neck end, then turn the turkey 180° and cut through the other side to remove the backbone (save it for making stock).

Very finely grind 2 Tbsp. whole black peppercorns and 2 Tbsp. whole pink or black peppercorns in a spice mill or mortar and pestle; transfer to a medium bowl. Add ½ cup Diamond Crystal or ¼ cup plus 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 2 Tbsp. garlic powder, 2 Tbsp. onion powder, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1 Tbsp. smoked paprika, and use your fingers to mix together.

Place turkey pieces, skin side up, on a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet. Sprinkle salt mixture liberally all over turkey, patting to adhere. You may not need all of it, but it’s good to have extra since some will end up on the baking sheet. Chill bird, uncovered, at least 24 hours and up to 2 days.

Remove turkey from wire rack and rinse baking sheet and rack if needed (turkey will most likely release some liquid). Line baking sheet with 3 layers of foil to make cleanup easy and set rack back inside. Arrange turkey pieces on rack, skin side up, and let sit at room temperature up to 2 hours to help decrease the cooking time.

Meanwhile, cook small handful of hardy herbs (such as sage, rosemary, bay leaves, and/or thyme), 4 garlic cloves, crushed, two 2x1" strips orange zest, ⅓ cup low-sodium soy sauce, ⅓ cup (packed; 71 g) light brown sugar, and ⅓ cup sherry vinegar or red wine vinegar in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until sugar is dissolved and glaze thickens slightly (it should just barely coat a spoon), 10–12 minutes. Remove glaze from heat.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Rub turkey with 6 Tbsp. neutral oil (such as vegetable, peanut, or canola) and pour 1 cup water into baking sheet. Roast turkey, rotating baking sheet halfway through, until skin is mostly golden brown, 20–25 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 300° and continue to roast turkey, brushing with glaze every 20 minutes and adding more water by ½-cupfuls as needed to maintain some liquid in baking sheet, until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of breast registers 150°, and 170° when inserted into the thickest part of the thighs, 50–70 minutes longer (total cooking time will be 1–1½ hours). Skin should be deep golden brown and shiny. Transfer turkey to a cutting board; tent loosely with foil. Let rest 30–60 minutes before carving.

If you're someone who would happily drive out of your way for Raising Cane's chicken fingers and a side of Cane's Sauce, your next order might be a whole lot closer to home.

The popular chicken chain is expanding in a pretty big way this November, with 12 new restaurants planned across 10 states. For some communities, it'll even be their first Raising Cane's location.

Nation's Restaurant News says the new markets include Brick, New Jersey; Fayetteville, North Carolina; and Sioux Falls, South Dakota, with the chain also adding restaurants in Alabama, California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Michigan, and Utah.

According to USA Today, the 12 restaurants are scheduled to open in the following cities throughout November:

For anyone unfamiliar with Raising Cane's, the chain has built its reputation around a fairly straightforward menu featuring chicken fingers, crinkle-cut fries, Texas toast, coleslaw, and its signature Cane's Sauce. Rather than offering dozens of different chicken sandwiches and menu combinations, Cane's keeps its focus on the essentials.

The chain is also picking up the pace with its openings. After adding seven restaurants in October, it's planning nearly twice as many for November, with the overall expansion as part of a much bigger growth push.

A recent rat study hinted that cosmic radiation could pose health risks for future Mars explorers. Live Science asks its readers whether they'd take the journey anyway.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A crewed mission to Mars could be one of humanity's greatest achievements, but getting there may come with serious health risks. Beyond the challenges of surviving in space for months at a time, astronauts would face prolonged exposure to cosmic radiation ‪—‬ high-energy particles in space that can penetrate the human body and potentially damage vital organs.

A new study suggested that cosmic radiation could pose a particular threat to heart health. Researchers found evidence that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what human astronauts might encounter during a mission to Mars and back developed more scar tissue around the small vessels in their hearts compared with rats that weren't exposed to space radiation.

Although the findings haven't been confirmed in humans yet, they add to the growing concerns about the long-term health effects of sending astronauts on long-duration space missions.

NASA and other space agencies are working on ways to eventually send humans to Mars and beyond. Given these latest findings, would you travel to Mars? Vote in the poll below, and let us know your thoughts in the comments.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. #6489. I’m So Obsessed With This Coffee Mug, I Tell Strangers About It

I wouldn't call myself a minimalist by any means, but I am not someone who buys a lot of kitchen gadgets or rushes to snag the latest seasonal cup. But ever since I picked up my first Fellow Carter Move Mug five years ago, I’ve happily repurchased it several times.

This sleek little mug, designed by the coffee nerds at Fellow, keeps your brew hot (or cold) without sacrificing flavor. I use it so often that I’ve sung its praises to a coffee shop owner in Washington, a bed-and-breakfast proprietor in Maine, and countless other strangers.

I love this mug more than I can express—so much, in fact, that I reached out to Fellow founder, Jake Miller, to chat about it. He launched the brand 13 years ago with the goal of delivering great design to coffee brewing, but customers kept asking for an exceptional way to drink their coffee on the go. So a company founded by and for coffee obsessives made the ultimate companion container.

The Carter Move Mug is designed with a superior drinking experience in mind. The body of the mug tapers into a thin drinking lip that Miller said was inspired by a wine glass. When you take a sip, you’re touching metal and not paint, and the lip is protected when the mug is closed.

At the time, other to-go cups were designed with a small opening in the lid and completely missed out on the aromatics. “It was a pretty opinionated design choice, but we wanted people to experience the incredible smells of coffee,” he explained. “Once the lid is off, you have this really great drinking experience.” While the lip of the mug is metal, the inside of the mug is ceramic-coated, so it doesn’t impart any taste to the coffee. According to Miller, “that allows for a more pure expression of the coffee.”

When I tell people about the Carter Mug, I like to joke that it’s almost too good at its job. Hot drinks stay very hot for hours, and I regularly find ice in the mug a full day after I first made my chilled version. I once left a mug of hot coffee in a car during a blizzard, and after almost a day, the coffee was still pleasant to drink. Miller said this effective temperature control is from two things: the distance between the two walls and how much vacuum insulation the mug has. Also, Fellow designed the lid to be gasket-tight so there’s minimal heat loss.

One of my favorite features of the Move Mug is the splash guard that clicks into the vessel and prevents big spills while you’re drinking in motion. (As a person prone to mess, this is very helpful.) This element, along with some other accessories, was born out of feedback based on how customers use their mugs, including a straw for cold coffee, a cup holder-friendly size, and the option for a slide top lid. “Everything we do is customer-driven,” Miller noted.

Maybe not important to how your coffee tastes — but important to aesthetics — the Move Mug is sleek and sophisticated, which means it’s suitable for most situations. There’s a nice range of colors, and it looks great in my hand on my commute and on my desk in the office. It’s truly the perfect accessory.

#6487. Ocean Spray Just Gave Canned Cranberry Sauce A Chocolate Makeover

Someone finally saw the potential in those jiggly, ridged slices.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Canned cranberry sauce has some pretty stiff competition at Thanksgiving. Between the mashed potatoes, stuffing, and mac and cheese, that jiggly little side dish often gets treated like the ugly stepsister of the dinner table. And it probably doesn't help that it comes out looking exactly like the can it was packaged in.

But perhaps a little chocolate could improve its reputation.

Ocean Spray and Los Angeles chocolatier Compartés have teamed up with recipe developer Carolina Gelen on a new treat called Chocolate Covered Cranberry Sauce, taking the familiar Ocean Spray stuff and turning it into chocolate-coated discs, sold in packs of four.

If that sounds vaguely familiar, you may have seen Gelen's original Instagram video from 2023, when she experimented with dipping slices of canned cranberry sauce in chocolate (the recipe has since racked up more than 10 million views).

Ocean Spray's Kelvin Vuong said Gelen's recipe was exactly the kind of unexpected use for cranberry sauce the company wanted to share with more people. The brand eventually partnered with her and Compartés to turn the homemade recipe into something people could purchase—and Gelen is pretty thrilled to see her original experiment come this far.

"Getting to work with Ocean Spray and Compartés to turn that idea into something people across the country can try is incredibly exciting," she said in the announcement.

As for why this combination works, Compartés' creative director and chief chocolatier, Jonathan Grahm, pointed to the contrast between the cranberries' sharp, sour flavor and the richness of the chocolate. It's the same reason tart fruit and chocolate can work so well together, even if cranberry sauce isn't exactly the first thing you'd think to dip.

The limited-edition chocolates are available exclusively at Compartés for $24.95 per four-pack, while supplies last, with the gourmet chocolate brand also making chocolate turkeys filled with Ocean Spray's whole-berry cranberry sauce in both milk and dark chocolate options.

Cranberry sauce might never get the same love as mashed potatoes, but chocolate certainly gives it a fighting chance.

A new mom experienced intense feelings of sadness whenever she breastfed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: About two weeks after her baby's birth, the woman began experiencing intensely negative emotions at every breastfeeding session. These feelings of "extreme unhappiness" would start just before her milk ejection reflex (during which milk moves from the breast ducts to the nipples) and last up to two minutes.

The feelings would end abruptly when she finished breastfeeding and then appear again the next time she was about to release milk, according to a report of the case, which the patient co-authored. The patient was a breastfeeding counselor for the United States Department of Agriculture Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) Program.

Until the baby was about 18 months old, this phenomenon would happen every time the woman breastfed — about five times per day, on average. Unlike postpartum depression,‬ which can cause persistent feelings of despondency, anxiety and mood swings in new parents,‬ the woman felt "helpless, hopeless, [and] worthless" only during her milk release. She reported that she otherwise felt happy and bonded with her new baby.

What happened next: When her baby was 7 months old, the woman began meeting with a lactation consultant, who later co-authored the case report. They worked together to track the mother's symptoms over time, noting when negative feelings began and if any intervention made them subside or worsen.

The diagnosis: Because the woman's condition did not have a formal name at the time, she began calling it "dysphoric milk ejection reflex," or D-MER.

The case report authors initially suspected that fluctuations in the woman's oxytocin levels might be causing D-MER, since the hormone is released into the bloodstream prior to the milk ejection reflex during breastfeeding. However, external factors that are known to affect oxytocin levels, such as tobacco use, did not always trigger the woman's symptoms.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Next, they looked at dopamine. The chemical messenger's fluctuations during breastfeeding are less studied than those of oxytocin and prolactin, another hormone linked to lactation. However, dopamine levels have otherwise been connected to strong emotional responses. Activities that seemed to ease the patient's D-MER symptoms — such as taking the cold medication pseudoephedrine, smoking cigarettes or binging on chocolate ice cream — are also known to increase dopamine levels. Meanwhile, acute stress, which reduces dopamine, worsened her symptoms.

The authors hypothesized that an abrupt drop in dopamine prior to milk release might be a trigger for D-MER.

D-MER differs from postpartum depression in that the feelings of sadness are very specific to lactation.

The treatment: The woman began taking bupropion (better known by the brand name Wellbutrin), an antidepressant that increases the amount of dopamine in the brain. She saw a dramatic reduction in her D-MER symptoms within a day, and five days later, her symptoms were almost entirely gone.

However, she stopped taking the drug after a few weeks due to unwanted side effects (which aren't described in the report), and the symptoms came back. She then tried an herbal remedy containing roseroot (Rhodiola rosea), a plant historically used in some places to manage depression. Some recent studies suggest that compounds in R. rosea interact with receptors for chemical messengers in the brain; however, there is little reliable evidence demonstrating its purported therapeutic benefits, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health.

She took R. rosea three to four times per day, reporting that her symptoms became "much milder" but returned if she skipped a day. As her daughter grew older and the woman breastfed less often, the woman stopped taking the supplement. When the child was 3 years old and no longer breastfeeding, the woman's D-MER symptoms went away entirely.

What makes the case unique: Prior to this report, published in 2011, D-MER was not widely recognized or documented in the scientific literature, and there was no research into its causes or treatment.

The patient and co-author of the report created the website D-MER.org in 2007 to share information about the condition more widely. She hoped to raise awareness among medical professionals and to help breastfeeding people who experience this condition by providing resources and support and encouraging them to understand that what they were feeling was a physiological side effect of nursing. Since the site's launch, hundreds of visitors have described having negative feelings while breastfeeding, according to the report.

Over the past two decades, more case reports describing the condition have been published. In a 2025 paper in the European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, researchers estimated that roughly 14.2% of lactating parents experience D-MER and that 1 in 6 stop breastfeeding as a result. Dopamine is thought to play a part, but the exact cause of D-MER has not been definitively established in peer-reviewed research yet.

There is no definitive treatment for D-MER, although some have anecdotally found relief through techniques for stress reduction, such as meditation and breathing exercises, and by seeking support from partners, friends and breastfeeding groups online.

Short-lived negative feelings resembling D-MER have also been reported in people who are not lactating. These anecdotal accounts describe intense, negative feelings brought on by nipple stimulation. One online discussion group referred to this phenomenon as "sad nipple syndrome," according to the authors of the case report. As with D-MER, dopamine may play a part, but the overall neurochemistry underlying that emotional response is unknown.

Breastfeeding and parenthood can be an emotional roller coaster even under the best circumstances, the authors noted. In that sense, they explained, people with D-MER have "the same emotional peaks and valleys" as all new parents do. Yet the negative feelings that accompany D-MER are nonetheless different from the normal range of emotions in the parents of newborns, and they can cause extreme distress if they are not correctly identified and addressed as being specific to breastfeeding.

People with D-MER, the authors concluded, "serve as a reminder to us all that we do not yet have a complete understanding of human lactation."

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Heise, A. M., & Wiessinger, D. (2011). Dysphoric milk ejection reflex: A case report. International Breastfeeding Journal, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.1186/1746-4358-6-6

With the film officially opening next month, restaurants and food brands have been busy giving us plenty of ways to spend our money before we've even bought a ticket. So whether you're a fellow Marvel obsessive or just someone who could use an excuse to order more donuts, here's a look at the Avengers: Doomsday food and drink collaborations you can find stateside.

Dunkin's massive Marvel collaboration launched November 4 with six themed drinks, including the Iced Captain'ccino, Doom Cloud Latte, and Wakandan Daydream Refresher, along with special donuts and MUNCHKINS. As if the drinks weren't enough to drain your wallet, collectible tumblers, mugs, cup sleeves, and even a Doctor Doom MUNCHKINS tin are also available to add to your collection. And if you happen to live in New York, Boston, Chicago, or Los Angeles, four Dunkin' restaurants are getting full Marvel makeovers beginning November 17.

Jack in the Box is feeding the entire team with its Doomsday Dipping Box, which packs popcorn chicken, mozzarella sticks, tacos, curly fries, a drink, and three dipping sauces—including the mysterious Assemble Sauce—into one meal. Available since November 5, the meal also comes with one of eight surprise magnets that fit together like puzzle pieces. If you're determined to collect the entire set, I hope you really like curly fries.

Dave & Buster's is committed to the superhero bit, going so far as to temporarily rename itself Doom & Buster's when the nationwide takeover officially begins November 16. It’ll bring Marvel-themed arcade experiences, prizes, collectible Power Cards, and five specialty drinks, including the Panther's Potion and Captain Punch mocktails. There's also DOOMHOUR, when rewards members can earn double tickets on eligible games during surprise one-hour windows, with the promotion running through January 31, 2027.

Considering Robert Downey Jr. co-founded happy coffee and is playing Doctor Doom, this partnership practically wrote itself. The brand has released eight collectible Marvel cans across four drinks: Classic Cold Brew, Tahitian Vanilla Cold Brew, Vanilla Latte, and Chocolatey Chip Latte. Each flavor features two character designs, including Doctor Doom, Thor, Gambit, and Mystique, and they're available online and at select retailers nationwide.

Even the M&M's characters are getting suited up. #6480. Pineapple Chaat

“Chaats are a mighty snack that tell India’s culinary story more adeptly than any other food,” writes Nashville-based Indian chef Maneet Chauhan in her cookbook Chaat. She reminisces about a fruity street snack sold by a chaat vendor near the Hyderabadi train station. Sweet pineapple, tangy lime juice, sour-salty chaat masala, chile powder, cilantro, and pomegranate seeds created what she describes as “a decadent mosaic of colors and plucky flavors.” Chauhan suggests swapping in ripe mango or watermelon when in season, or drizzling the finished dish with lightly salted yogurt for added richness and depth. Serve as a snack, or as a side dish for barbecued meats or seafood.

#6479. BA Bake Club Has Your Holiday Showstopper Covered

Lucky you: We’re sharing December’s BA Bake Club drop early so you can get started on holiday planning right…now!

For members of Bon Appétit Bake Club, every month is filled with special treats, but the holiday season calls for something bigger, grander, even more spectacular. This Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake ticks every box. And it’s just enough of a challenge to ensure you feel accomplished. The one-bowl chocolate cake is dense and deeply fudgy; the mousse is airy and light; and the thin slip of ganache on top brings it all together. No matter what kind of year you’ve had, this dessert is the way to cap it all off. Here’s how to make it:

This mousse has three foundational pastry techniques hidden in plain sight. It starts with a crème anglaise, a lusciously pourable custard. Adding that to a bowl of chopped chocolate yields a crémeux, a velvety and dense emulsified custard. Folding in whipped cream finally turns it into a fluffy mousse. Magical.

It’s important to use a 70% chocolate here. It’s intense enough to shine through the heavy cream and has enough cocoa butter to provide structure and stability, ensuring the mousse doesn’t slump.

A springform pan is a worthy and necessary investment, ensuring an anxiety-free presentation. It also allows you to bake and build the cake in just one tin.

For an architectural slice that looks like it strutted out of a fancy patisserie, dip the blade of your knife in hot water, then wipe it clean with a dry kitchen towel between each cut.

#6478. Weather Guard’s Pack Rat Turned My Nephew's Pickup Into a Rolling Workshop

Instead of digging through tool bags and loose hardware at every stop, the Pack Rat Drawer Unit kept everything organized, secure, and within easy reach—making every job site a little more efficient.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Let’s start with a bit of transparency here: When Weather Guard sent me its Pack Rat truck toolbox, I thought it was destined for my new Honda Ridgeline. Then reality set in. While the Ridgeline is a fantastic daily driver and weekend project truck, its composite bed and in-bed trunk make it a poor match for a permanently mounted contractor toolbox. That trunk alone is a vehicle highlight, so burying it beneath a steel monolith seemed almost criminal. So instead of writing a review based on specs alone, I handed the Pack Rat over to someone who actually needed it—my nephew, a newly minted electrician who spends his days hauling electrical tools, fittings, wire, and hardware from one job site to the next.

A few hours after we installed it into his pickup and began organizing his gear, it became obvious this wasn’t just another truck accessory. It fundamentally changed how he uses his truck.

Picture a broad, low steel box bolted to the pickup bed’s floor, with a single wide drawer that pulls out over the lowered tailgate. The model we tested measures 60 inches long by 49½ inches wide, and stands 9½ inches tall. At that expanse, the top of the box system essentially becomes the new carry bed of the truck, sitting just about level with the wheel wells.

That measurement is something to be mindful of if you carry a lot of taller cargo. Trucks vary in cargo bed depth, so you’ll have to subtract 9½ inches from the overall depth of your bed to know the remaining height to the top of your bed rails. The top of the bed rails on my nephew’s Chevy Silverado 1500 sits at around 21 inches, so he still has a substantial 11½ inches to carry cargo.

To that end, for the model we tested—the 369-3-04—Weather Guard rates the top for up to 2,000 pounds evenly distributed. The drawer itself has a separate 425-pound capacity. That’s a lot of weight. It should be noted that your truck’s payload limit still applies to the combined weight of the box—about 300 pounds—its contents, and any cargo on top.

The Pack Rat is less a toolbox and more like a mobile organization system. Beneath the steel top, a massive full-width drawer rides on a set of internal rollers that allow it to glide smoothly in spite of the load within. Fully loaded with cordless tools and hardware, the drawer never sagged or bounced once. To that end, we thought pushing it shut would be a chore, but the drawer rolled back in with little effort, closing with an authoritative thunk that spoke to the solid overall build quality. It’s the kind of rolling momentum that reminds you to keep your fingers clear–not because it’s flawed in any way, but because it’s built with serious heft.

Organization is where the Pack Rat really makes its mark. Four walls fixed across the drawer space are separated by 24 adjustable divider panels. This allows you to tailor the drawer layout to fit your needs instead of forcing your tools into compartments of predetermined size. My nephew dedicated one side almost entirely to his Milwaukee cordless tool collection–drills, impact drivers, oscillating tool, batteries, and chargers–while configuring the remaining space to hold electrical supplies that change from job to job. Connectors, wire nuts, fittings, fasteners, electrical tape, and specialty tools all have designated homes, making it immediately obvious when he is in low supply on any item.

Weather Guard also paid attention to the details outside the drawer. The top surface is lined with aggressive grip tape, providing secure footing when climbing into the truck bed on damp mornings or during inclement weather. It seems like a small touch until you realize you’ll be stepping on this box as a platform throughout the day.

Before installing the Pack Rat, my nephew would often toss fittings, connectors, and hand tools into half a dozen different bags and bins. Now everything lives in one place, where it stays dry as a bone. He spends less time digging through piles of tools, knows exactly where everything belongs, and can get back to work faster. For professionals whose trucks serve as rolling workshops, those small gains in efficiency translate into real money saved over the course of months and years.

The Pack Rat is unapologetically designed for tradespeople–or at least serious enthusiasts whose vehicles are dedicated to their everyday work life. It’s a substantial piece of equipment, and that comes with trade-offs. The heavy-gauge steel construction adds noticeable weight to your vehicle, which will inevitably have some impact on your vehicle’s fuel economy. Installation is more involved than dropping, say, a Tmat organizing system or cross-over box into the bed since it’s meant to stay put. Furthermore, once installed the box consumes roughly 7 to 8 inches of vertical bed space. The tradeoff, of course, is that you retain the entire footprint of the bed above it. But if you frequently haul taller gear or equipment, that’s something to consider.

For the right buyer, though, those compromises will likely fade into the background. For years, my own truck was my office, my warehouse, my livelihood—even my diner most days. So it would have been a joy—and a value add—to have the Pack Rat at that stage of my work life. At the end of the day, having every tool, fastener, and accessory protected, organized, and within arm’s reach isn’t just convenient—it’s a real productivity upgrade.

Paul Russell Smith is a former NYC ironworker turned screenwriter (Grace Point) and home renovation specialist. He lives in a crooked old farmhouse in Stockton, NJ, where he’s just as likely to be clearing a clogged pipe as rewriting a third act. When he’s not working, he enjoys hiking, pedestrian beer, and cooking over a live fire. His self-proclaimed spirit animal is the English Bulldog.

The sale of the Nanotyrannus "Jodi" for over $47 million shines a stark light on the commodification of Earth's history. By selling dinosaurs off to the highest bidder, we lose what makes them valuable in the first place.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dinosaurs are more than extraordinary specimens with massive price tags. They are irreplaceable snapshots of our planet's history and our own human journey. When scientifically important fossils are reduced to luxury commodities, we are robbed of the evidence that makes them valuable in the first place.

On Oct. 27, a 19.6-foot-long (6 meters) skeleton of Nanotyrannus lancensis known as "Jodi" was sold at Sotheby's in New York for $47,255,000, far exceeding its $6 million to $9 million estimate. The buyer and seller were not identified. It was the latest in a string of multimillion-dollar dinosaur auctions, following the $50.1 million sale of a T. rex (Gus) in July and the $44.6 million sale of a Stegosaurus (Apex) in 2024.

Fossils like Jodi, Apex, and Gus belong in public collections, where they can contribute to science and remain accessible for future generations. Not in the hands of private collectors.

There are three main reasons why. First: Fossils are evidence, not objects. A dinosaur's bones can reveal how it grew, moved, fed, and lived. They preserve traces of injury and disease, help reconstruct ancient ecosystems, and offer clues about the "rules of life" governing our world that scientists are still learning to interpret.

Jodi illustrates exactly why access to physical evidence matters. For nearly half a century, paleontologists debated whether Nanotyrannus was a distinct dinosaur or simply a juvenile T. rex. A lack of well-preserved fossils available for study only fueled the uncertainty. And then a remarkable specimen, once in private hands, moved into the public trust.

The fossil was uncovered in Montana in 2006 alongside a Triceratops. Dubbed the "Dueling Dinosaurs," it took until 2022, and an appeal in the state's Supreme Court, for the remains to be acquired by the Museum of Natural Sciences so they could be fully studied. This research provided a powerful new perspective, arguing that Nanotyrannus lancensis was a distinct dinosaur and, moreover, that a second species of Nanotyrannus once roamed the American West.

When access relies on a private owner's permission, repeatability is not assured, and science cannot proceed. A specimen might be available today but inaccessible tomorrow.

This hypothesis has big implications for the health of ecosystems before one of Earth's most severe extinction events — but it currently rests on the scant few Nanotyrannus specimens housed in public collections. Specimens like Jodi could uphold or dethrone it. Without access, we, and Jodi’s true identity, will remain in the dark.

It is hard to overstate the irony of Jodi's sale: a specimen recently listed as a juvenile T. rex now captures the world's imagination, and commands double the price tag, as a "Nanotyrannus." Yet if a similar fate had befallen the Dueling Dinosaurs and they had remained in private hands, we would not have known for certain that Nanotyrannus ever existed.

Scientific progress depends on researchers being able to compare specimens, test hypotheses, and revisit earlier conclusions. When access relies on a private owner's permission, repeatability is not assured, and science cannot proceed. A specimen might be available today but inaccessible tomorrow. This is why access to the evidence must endure.

This brings us to the second problem with privately owned dinosaurs. Digital scans cannot replace the original fossil.

Three-dimensional scans and digital models are powerful tools. We use them to measure bones, compare anatomy, share information, and educate the public. But digital models capture only the most superficial aspects of a fossil's story.

The auction took place on Oct. 27, with Jodi eventually selling for around five times the top estimate.

To understand dinosaur growth, we examine microscopic structures inside fossilized bone through a technique called bone histology. We also analyze the chemistry of fossils to investigate diet, migration patterns, and metabolism. Such work requires physical samples, not just images of a bone's surface. We also need contextual data about the surrounding sediments, preservation mode, and ancient environment in order to explore questions about the ecosystems in which the animals once lived. Much of this information is lost in the rush to excavate and prepare fossils as quickly as possible for the auction block. It can never be reclaimed.

We cannot predict what novel technologies future researchers will employ to make new discoveries from old bones, or even which questions they will ask. Technology will continue to advance, bringing analytical methods we cannot anticipate. A scan made today does not guarantee that researchers will have the physical evidence needed for tomorrow's discoveries. Digital access should complement preservation of original specimens, not justify losing it.

Finally, private ownership cannot guarantee lasting public access. Yes, some private collectors financially support research and education and donate specimens they purchase. Those contributions are valuable. But the issue is not whether an individual owner is generous; it is whether access is guaranteed over time.

A temporary loan is insufficient. A loaned specimen can be withdrawn, sold, or inherited by someone with different priorities, situations that are becoming increasingly common in the U.S. and abroad. By contrast, a fossil deposited in a responsible public research institution is documented, cared for, studied, and made available to future researchers and educators in perpetuity. The question is not whether people should be able to admire dinosaurs; it is whether the evidence that helps us understand them will remain available to everyone.

Nor should museums consider selling scientifically important fossils to cover operating shortfalls. Collections are not ordinary financial assets to liquidate when budgets tighten. Selling an irreplaceable specimen provides a one-time payment while sacrificing future scientific potential. Museums need sustainable funding for collections care, research, and education, not pressure to trade away the very resources they exist to preserve.

Jodi's sale is complete, but the fossil's long-term future remains uncertain. With the buyer's identity undisclosed, the public cannot know what arrangements, if any, will ensure continued access for researchers and educators. We hope the new owner will make Jodi available for scientific study and public education, through permanent placement in a public research institution. But hope is not a substitute for a guarantee.

There is a better way to support paleontology. Enthusiasts who want to share in the excitement of discovery can fund fieldwork and research, endow curatorial positions, strengthen museum collections, or donate important fossils to public institutions where we can all learn from them.

Dinosaurs inspire wonder because they connect us to a world vastly different from our own. But their importance extends far beyond their power to captivate us. They are part of our shared natural heritage and an irreplaceable record of Earth's history.

We should measure a dinosaur's worth not by the price it commands at auction, but by the knowledge it can help us build, and by whether we preserve that opportunity for generations to come. Earth's history belongs to all of us, not to the highest bidder.

Editor's note: This article was updated on Nov. 4 at 8.22 a.m. ET to correct the year the Museum of Natural Sciences acquired the Dueling Dinosaurs.

#6475. Goat Kari

Food writer Rachel Gurjar made this goat kari for her “lifelong idol” Madhur Jaffrey, the renowned Indian cookbook author, at a dinner Gurjar hosted in her Brooklyn apartment in September 2022. When Jaffrey asked for the recipe, Gurjar knew she had to include it in her debut cookbook, East to East.

You can find goat meat at your local halal butcher or substitute lamb. If opting for goat, Gurjar recommends requesting a bone-in “curry cut,” which means the butcher will cut the meat into 2- to 3-inch pieces that are ideal for braising.

While you can use store-bought garam masala, Gurjar always DIYs her own spice blend inspired by the one her mother used to make back in India. “It’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional,” she writes. “This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again.” You can also customize your blend: Add more cinnamon and fennel for a sweeter garam masala, or up the black pepper and cloves for a spicier kick.
