#6430. A 400-Year-Old Mass Murderer Led a Brutal Mutiny—and Became the First Corporate Psychopath

A modern psychopathy test, applied to a 1629 shipwreck, uncovers the dark origins of toxic bosses.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

When you try to envision a “corporate psychopath,” the kind of individual who blends charm towards their superiors and sadism towards their subordinates to rise through the corporate ranks, who comes to mind?

Actually, don’t say a specific name. These guys can be very litigious, so let’s just focus on the vague and the deceased. You’re probably picturing a man in an expensive business suit, maybe having a loud, hyperbolic conversation on an oversized 1980s cell phone. Maybe he’s monologuing about how “greed is good,” or how they’re “gonna need to send the National Guard to take him out, ‘cause he’s not goin’ nowhere.” Perhaps the corporate psychopath you have in mind is busy fretting about whether his business card has lettering in Romalian or Silian Rail.

In other words, short of someone you’ve seen on the news, or in your own boardroom, your mental image of a corporate psychopath probably comes from the movies.

You may want to revise that. That’s because a new study suggests that the original corporate psycho predates the 1980s stock market antiheroes of the movies you love. He actually predates movies entirely. In fact, he died before the city of Boston was ever founded.

In a study published in the Asian Journal of Business Ethics, Clive Roland Boddy, an author and pioneer in the study of corporate psychopathy, has identified Jeronimous Cornelisz of the Dutch East India Company as perhaps the earliest documented example of a corporate psychopath. To understand why, one must delve into the dark story of the 1629 Batavia shipwreck and its mutinous aftermath.

The Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie, translated as Dutch East India Company and abbreviated as VOC, was a fairly unique venture in the business world at the dawn of the 17th century. At the time, expeditions for goods and resources were often funded individually, and the companies behind them lasted only as long as a single voyage. The VOC changed that by merging 12 existing “pre-companies” within the Dutch Republic into a permanent company that would not only fund spice expeditions but also manage supply and stabilize the market. Shares of the VOC could be publicly purchased and traded by Dutch citizens at various aftermarkets throughout the Republic, including the predecessor to the Euronext Amsterdam, arguably making the VOC the world’s first multinational corporation.

In some ways, the VOC resembled the multinational corporations we know today, with the same ruthless efficiency. Yet the world around it lacked the kind of laws and regulations that are at least supposed to keep the corporations of our modern world in check. In fact, the Dutch government backed the VOC entirely, allowing the company to have a monopoly over the Asian spice trade. It was an environment that favored the bold, the ambitious, and the unscrupulous. It was an environment that allowed a man like Jeronimus Cornelisz to seize his moment.

“Psychopaths have a narcissistic and grossly inflated view of their self-worth and importance,” Mike Dash writes in his book Batavia’s Graveyard: The True Story of the Mad Heretic Who Led History’s Bloodiest Mutiny, “...a truly astonishing egocentricity and sense of entitlement, and see themselves as the centre of the universe, as superior beings who are justified in living according to their own rules.” It’s unclear exactly when Jeronimus Cornelisz created his own set of rules to live by, whether in his poorly-documented childhood, or when he took up his apothecary trade some time in the 1620s and began battling with his local town council.

What we know is that by 1628, the death of his child and the subsequent scandal it invited (the three-month old had died of syphilis, and Cornelisz tried to argue the child had contracted it from a wet nurse rather than his own wife) led to the Dutchman selling his business and taking a job with the VOC. In October 1628, the Batavia left port in the Netherlands on a trip to the Dutch East Indies, with commodore Francisco Pelsaert as its commander, Ariaen Jacobsz as its skipper, and Cornelisz as a junior officer.

Pelsaert’s journal recounts that on June 4, 1629, “I was lying in my bunk feeling ill and felt suddenly, with a rough terrible movement, the bumping of the ship’s rudder, and immediately after that I felt the ship held up in her course against the rocks, so that I fell out of my bunk.” The vessel had run aground on Western Australia’s Morning Reef while Jacobsz was at the helm, and roughly 100 of the 340 people aboard the ship were killed in the collision. To date, there’s still fierce debate over whether the Batavia crashed “by design or accident,” as by this time, Cornelisz had charmed his way into Jacobsz’ esteem, and in doing so, had convinced him that a mutiny was necessary to depose Pelsaert.

Either way, as some of the roughly 180 survivors disembarked for the nearby islands, leaving only 70 (including Cornelisz) aboard, an opportunity arose for the original “hostile takeover.”

Cornelisz had originally been among the 70 or so who remained aboard the Batavia, but after nine days, he made his way to nearby Beacon Island. He found the survivors stranded there to be starving, dying of thirst, and feeling abandoned, since Pelsaert had left with the other officers in search of supplies and aid. Seizing his moment, Cornelisz stepped into the leadership vacuum, amassing a group of loyal enforcers, and stripping the now subordinate survivors of any means by which to fend for, or defend, themselves.

Cornelisz began a reign of terror that lasted more than two months, overseeing the execution of those deemed “too weak,” as well as those he thought capable of overpowering him. Supplies were hoarded for his loyalists, while those outside of his circle were dispatched in ever more public and brutal ways. His roughly 40 man cadre killed an estimated 100-125 men, women, and children, and the survivors didn’t fare much better.

“Furthermore, when the most murders had been committed,” Pelseart would write in his journal, “...they shared the women who remained, or rather whom they had meant to stay alive.” Cornelisz, who had singled out Lucretia Jansz for his own ill-intent, “made several articles to which the women had to be put on oath if they wanted to remain alive, that they had to be obedient to the men in all that they should desire of them.”

While all of this may read like the barbaric horrors of a bygone age, befitting a pirate’s pillaging more than a modern boardroom, Boddy’s study found that when Cornelisz’s actions are viewed through the prism of The Psychopathy Measure–Management Research Version (PM–MRV), a ten-item model he previously developed to identify contemporary corporate psychopaths, the mutinous, murderous junior officer of the VOC checked off every box.

Boddy’s article doesn’t recontextualize Cornelisz’s crimes to exonerate the man; there’s little debate that Jeronimus was a psychopath of some stripe. Nor does Boddy suggest that the existence of the VOC created or caused Cornelisz’s monstrous urges. Rather, it emphasizes that the profit motive built into the structure of the VOC “would have been too great, even for a careful primary psychopath” to resist. This analysis demonstrates that corporate psychopaths as we know them today “have been active since the start of the World’s first stock exchange, and first multinational shareholder-owned corporations.” What unites Cornelisz with the less-overtly-murderous corporate psychopaths we encounter today is the manner in which they both “utilise a similar modus operandi across the centuries and are motivated by greed, self-aggrandisement, and the desire to hurt, dominate and control others.”

In other words, to subvert a quote lamented by another lunatic, Billy Loomis in 1996’s Scream: corporations don’t create psychos. Corporations make psychos more creative.

#6429. China Unveils Their Plan for a Crewed Moon Landing

Yesterday, on November 3rd, the deputy chief designer of China's crewed space program and chief designer of the lunar exploration program (Wang Xiang) unveiled an official statement detailing its plans for a crewed mission to the Moon. Under the proposed architecture, China will conduct two launches using the Long March 10 rocket, sending the Lanyue lunar lander and the Mengzhou crewed spaceship to the Moon, where they will rendezvous in orbit. Of the three taikonaut crew, two will then transfer from the spaceship to the lander and descend to the surface to conduct science operations.

The plans were outlined in a keynote speech Wang delivered at the 7th Manned Space Symposium, held from Oct. 31st to Nov.1st at Beihang University in Beijing. This year's theme was "Gathering Wisdom for the Galaxy: Digital and Intelligent Empowerment for High-Quality Development of Manned Spaceflight," and saw more than 800 experts and scholars from fields related to crewed spaceflight convene to discuss strategies, technologies, and the hurdles China's space program will face.

These plans echo the preliminary plan statements made at the 9th China (International) Commercial Aerospace Forum in July 2023. As Deputy chief engineer Zhang Hailian of the China Manned Space Engineering (CMSE) office said at the time, two Long March-10 rockets would launch the elements to the Moon separately. Zhang's slideshow also included a rendering of a lander depicted on a mural inside China's Manned Lunar Deep Exploration Project Office.

The CMSE unveiled the lander design to the world in September 2023 and officially named it Lanyue ("embracing the Moon") in early 2024. Since then, development of the Long March 10, Mengzhou spacecraft, and Lanyue lander has proceeded apace and reached several key milestones. This included a tethered test of the lander last year, which successfully simulated descent, guidance, control, and engine shutdown.

The Mengzhou spacecraft also successfully completed a series of zero-height abort and maximum dynamic pressure escape tests in June 2025 while the Long March-10 successfully completed a low-altitude demonstration and validation test earlier this year. These developmental milestones place China on track to complete a crewed lunar mission by 2030.

In an interview with China's state-controlled media company, CCTV, Wang said that their planning approach follows two principles and will consist of using different vehicle variants for different stages. To prepare for rendezvous in lunar orbit, China will use the Tiangong space station in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) to validate the rockets, lander and space capsule. An uncrewed flight mission of the Lanyue lander will also happen before a crew landing is attempted, which will gather critical environmental data on the luanr surface.

In addition, Wang highlighted how in preparation for crewed missions, the mission components will all be tested in an uncrewed state first:

We will use the near-Earth version of the Long March 10 to launch the near-Earth version of the Mengzhou spacecraft to perform space station missions in Low-Earth Orbit, validating the rocket's basic technologies and the critical re-entry and return phases of the spacecraft. Then we will use the lunar version of the Long March 10 to launch the lunar version of the Mengzhou spacecraft to execute the lunar landing mission. This is the validation process for the rocket: near-Earth first, then the Moon.

Artist's recreation of the two Chinese spacecraft that will put 'taikonauts' on the Moon. Credit: CSM

For the near-Earth phase of the plan, the Long March 10A (CZ 10A) will be used, a single stick variant with only two stages and no boosters. For the lunar mission, the standard, three-stage variant with additional boosters will be used, which has a payload capacity of 27 metric tons (~30 U.S. tons). This process is virtually identical to what NASA has been pursuing with its Artemis Program. Initially, NASA hoped to use the Block 2 variant of the Space Launch System (SLS) to deliver crew and payloads to the lunar surface (which has since been cancelled).

China's incremental "near-Earth first, then the Moon" approach is also very similar to the NASA's current launch plans. Before a crewed Orion spacecraft flew four astronauts around the Moon with Artemis II, NASA launched the uncrewed Artemis I capsule on a circumlunar flight to validate all the key systems. China's stated plans for an orbital rendezvous is also similar to NASA's revised plans for the Artemis III mission scheduled for next year, involving the seperate launch and an Orion spacecraft with a yet-to-be-determined Human Landing System (HLS).

"In an uncrewed state, we will validate many key technologies of the entire crewed process as possible, including launch, orbiting the Moon, docking with the Mengzhou spacecraft, landing and staying on the lunar surface, taking off again, and re-docking with the Mengzhou spacecraft," Wang added. "This is to ensure that the crewed flight is safe and reliable." Wang further indicated that the program has established system plans, technical standards and quality requirements under a single development framework.

China's long-term vision includes the creation of an International Lunar Research Station, the construction of which is currently planned to commence in 2031 using the super heavy-lift Long March 9 rockets. Roscosmo's involvement in the project is unclear at this time due to Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine and the way this has led to record lows in terms of annual launches and delays in the super-heavy Yenisei rocket. The details of this base are sitll somewhat vague, with the stated description claiming it will be located on the surface or in orbit.

#6428. Exoplanets Can't Hide From The JWST's 'Digital Twin'

Exoplanets would be a lot easier to find if so many of them weren't so close to stars. But they are, and that's something exoplanet scientists have to contend with. Coronagraphs do great work blocking out starlight and making dim planets more visible, but they have their limitations.

The JWST has coronagraphic capabilities embedded in its NIRCam (Near-Infrared Camera) and MIRI (Mid-Infrared Instrument). These capabilities have helped the JWST study some tough subjects hidden in the glare of stars, like debris disks, and to observe extremely luminous objects like quasars.

But all telescopes have a stability limit, even the steady-eyed JWST. The stability limit is a threshold beyond which mechanical, thermal, or optical fluctuations make clear images impossible. The JWST has fine guidance sensors and a 5-layer sunshield to raise this threshold, but the limit is still there.

New research in Nature explains how astronomers developed a way to subtract more starlight from the JWST's observations and image exoplanets that are up against the telescope's limits. It's titled "Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit," and the lead author is Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez. Ferrero-Chavez is a graduate student in the Department of Physics & Astronomy at Northwestern University.

"Exoplanet imaging is the main method for detailed characterization of planets orbiting beyond 1âau (astronomical unit) but it requires suppressing the bright glare of the star to see the faint planet light," the authors write. Suppressing that glare requires a couple of things, including extremely stable telescopes.

âWe try to make telescopes extremely stable, but there are extreme engineering challenges that we havenât quite solved yet,â said study co-author Jason Wang, assistant professor of physics and astronomy at Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences at NW. âThere are known causes of instability and unknown causes. Small thermal changes could cause a mirror to expand or contract by a picometer. Telescopes like JWST have cryocoolers to keep the instrument super cold. Those coolers have little motors that can cause the mirrors to vibrate. So, there are issues like those but also issues that we still donât understand as we learn how to build these complex telescopes.â

But a stable telescope is only part of the picture. Image processing plays a huge role in modern astronomy, and the two factors, telescope stability and image processing, play into each other.

"As well as sophisticated instrumentation, effective image processing is necessary for starlight suppression, which continues to be a substantial limitation," the authors write.

There are standard algorithms that astronomers employ to overcome this limitation, including using reference images to model starlight.

âFor the past 20 years, astronomers have tackled this problem by observing a different star and using its image as a reference,â said Wang said. âThen, they subtract that reference image from the original observation to remove the unwanted glare to reveal faint planets that otherwise might be hidden.â

This image shows how the JWST uses coronagraphic masks in MIRI and NIRCam to remove starlight. The white star marks the location of the real star and illustrates how it's been effectively removed from the image. It's effective, but the new method will increase its effectiveness and reveal even dimmer exoplanets. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, Alyssa Pagan (STScI); Science: ERS 1386 Team, Aarynn Carter (UC Santa Cruz)

But reference images have their limits too. That method still suffers from inevitable instabilities in a telescope that arise when switching from a reference image to an actual observation. Overcoming these stubborn obstacles will mean we can directly image more exoplanets.

"Addressing this challenge will increase the number of planets amenable to direct imaging and will be a notable step towards imaging exo-Earths with future observatories," the researchers explain.

Their answer is a new method based on physics and modelling that also borrows ideas from machine-learning. It can account for the JWST's tiny, nanoscale imperfections. The method lets astronomers subtract starlight from images more effectively than ever before.

âPlanets are a million times fainter than their stars,â said lead author Ferrer-Chavez. âSo, to image exoplanets, we need to remove that glare. That is a very tricky problem because even the tiniest changes in the telescope can affect how that glare appears. Slight shifts or tilts â even on the scale of just a few nanometers â can change the pattern of light. Our method models how light travels through the telescope and accounts for those tiny changes, allowing us to remove the glare much more precisely.â

This comes down to PSF, point spread function. Every telescope detects light imperfectly. They all distort or bend light in some way. So instead of a point source appearing as a point, it inevitably is degraded somehow. That can hide extremely dim sources like exoplanets in the glare of their stars. Accounting for PSF is a work-a-day part of astronomy.

The new system is called FLIP, (Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets) and it overcomes the problem of switching from reference images to real observations. FLIP "incorporates a multistep optimization strategy with a flexible physical model informed by wavefront sensing data to achieve the PSF fidelity necessary for real data," the authors write.

That's more technical detail than many will find interesting. But this type of work is behind the gorgeous images and fascinating discoveries in astronomy.

(a) shows the usual method of subtracting starlight from observations using reference images. Those image are imperfect and when combined with telescope stability, faint exoplanets remain hidden. (b) shows FLIP. Rather than reference images, it uses a differentiable instrument model and a physics based starlight model rather than an empirical starlight model. That means that starlight is more effectively removed from the end image, and a faint exoplanet becomes visible. Hooray! Image Credit: Ferrer-Chavez, R., Wang, J.J., Bouman, K.L. et al. Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit. Nature 659, 58â62 (2026).

In essence, the researchers created what they're calling a "digital twin" of the JWST with FLIP. The twin reproduces how light travels through the JWST down to the smallest detail. It includes subtle shifts, distortions, and imperfections. They repeatedly adjusted FLIP until it matched the JWST's real observations, including the polluting starlight. After that, they subtracted the star's glare from the image.

They tested it on 51 Eridani b, an exoplanet found with ground-based telescopes. The usual image processing techniques couldn't see the exoplanet hidden in the glare when observed at the wavelength that the JWST uses to find CO2 in exoplanet atmospheres. (They chose that wavelength because that's a critical part of the JWST's job, and a sort of sweet spot in its capabilities.)

But when the researchers used FLIP, the planet came into view.

Left: JWST/NIRCam observation of star 51 Eridani A (51 Eri) in the F430M filter, using a standard processing method named KLIPto subtract the glare of the star. This method was not able to detect the planet 51 Eri b in the original analysis, whose expected location is marked with a dashed circle. Middle: The same observation, but using new method FLIP to subtract the glare of the star. Astrophysicists obtained a significant detection (>5 sigma) of 51 Eri b. Right: Simulated image of 51 Eri b, highlighting that the planet is detected at its expected location and that the planet signal has the expected morphology. The location of the star 51 Eri is marked with a star symbol. Image credit: Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez.

"We achieve sensitivity 2â15 times superior to standard techniques, including the first detection of 51âEridaniâb at 4.3âÎ¼m," the authors write. "This is the first time, to our knowledge, that such an approach has demonstrated substantially improved sensitivity on real, on-sky coronagraphic imaging."

âWe showed that we can actually recover a planet that people previously couldnât see,â Wang said. âThis is real data in a real scenario. It was science left on the table because we didnât have the right tools to analyze the data in the most optimal way.â

FLIP seems to have a bright future. Not only with the JWST, but with other space telescopes like the Habitable Worlds Observatory. Imaging exo-Earths with the HWO, for example, will require extreme stability, and FLIP might get us there. In fact, FLIP might make the HWO more easy to design and build.

"In this work, we have shown sensitivity beyond the stability limit in JWSTâNIRCam," the authors write. "If this can be extended to HWO contrast levels, the ultrastability requirement for the system may be partially lifted, with the error budget necessary for image post-processing being reduced, and thus the design of the observatory may become more tractable."

In short, FLIP can take some of the pressure off of the engineering challenges in building more and more powerful telescopes, and can help overcome their stability limits.

âWe know of no planets around other stars that are like those in our own solar system,â Ferrer-Chavez said. âItâs not that they donât exist. Itâs that we cannot see them. Every time we improve our techniques, we discover new types of planets. By finding more planets, we can better understand how planetary systems form and evolve, and ultimately how typical our own solar system truly is.â

#6427. Sticky Miso Chicken

Miso, soy, and honey are a powerful trio, creating a savory marinade that could make just about anything sing (cod or salmon, broccoli or zucchini, tofu). Do have a keen eye on your chicken (especially if you have a drawer-style broiler at the bottom of your oven), checking it every so often to prevent a completely blackened cook.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: My Go-To Marinade for Chicken Is 3 Ingredients.

Heat broiler. Whisk ¼ cup honey, ¼ cup white miso, and 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a large bowl to combine. Add 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (the miso and soy sauce are plenty salty, so no need to season the chicken) and toss to coat. Arrange on wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet lined with foil and spoon any marinade remaining in bowl over. Broil chicken, turning halfway through, until cooked through and deeply charred in spots, 10–15 minutes (keep a close eye on it). Thinly slice chicken. Serve over steamed white rice, topped with thinly sliced scallions, if desired.

#6426. Mexican Seafood and Natural Wines Are in the Spotlight at This New NYC Restaurant

A stacked tuna tostada, puckering shrimp aguachile, and more seafood dishes stun at El Camarón Peludo

Known for their roasted and slow-cooked meats at Taqueria Ramirez, Tania Apolinar and Giovanni Cervantes partnered with chef Carlos Barrera to open a new seafood-focused wine bar this year. Here’s what a full day of prep looks like at El Camarón Peludo in the West Village.

First, fresh shrimp from Sinaloa, Mexico; Ecuador; and more locales are de-shelled and de-veined for three central shrimp dishes. Then, Cervantes starts the fresh salsa for the day, taste testing and comparing each batch to the salsa from last week to make sure the flavor is consistent. A bright red salsa is mixed with mayo to create the sauce on the camarones zarandeados, a shrimp version of a fish dish from the Pacific coast of Mexico that is usually grilled in a flat wire grill basket.

Upstairs, Apolinar prepares the wine bar for opening, laying out chilled seafood on ice in the window and wine bottles that will be placed in chilled buckets for service. She recommends sitting at the long, winding bar to watch the bartenders and chefs work.

Back in the kitchen, Barrera starts breaking down Spanish tuna for a creative tuna tostada layered with spicy mayo, fish eggs, habanero-lime oil, avocado, and crispy leeks. Then it’s taco prep, including the pescadilla (a deep-fried fish taco) and a shrimp taco with queso fresco, refried beans, and slices of roasted poblano peppers. Cervantes and Barrera prep the raw bar area, making salsa verde and salsa negro. The green salsa is made with parsley while the black salsa is layered with habaneros, piquin chile, and squid ink.

Cervantes explains that his original idea to pair the innovative seafood plates with bubbly wine turned into a natural wine bar, with El Camarón Peludo sourcing bottles from all over the world.

Watch the team at the Mexican seafood wine bar prepare tostadas, tacos, and flavor-packed aguachile in the newest episode of Now Open.

#6425. Interstellar Visitor 3I/ATLAS Shows Water Ice Behaves the Same Across Alien Star Systems

Targets of opportunity sometimes happen in astronomy, and we got a major one when the third interstellar object, 3I/ATLAS, was discovered in July 2025. And it just so happens that in the intervening years between the last known interstellar visitor (2I/Borisov in 2019), we got a major upgrade in our observational capabilities with the launch of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). A new paper from a team of researchers led by Dr. Silvia Protopapa of NASAâs Goddard Space Flight Center and the Southwest Research Institute, and published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, details JWSTâs findings on the water ice content of this most recent visitor from beyond our solar system.

Typically, water ice is pretty easy to spot for astronomers. In infrared, which is JWSTâs specialty, it absorbs light very clearly at 1.5, 2.0, and 3.0 microns in wavelength. Weâve known that for years, and have seen evidence of it in regular comets based strictly on our solar system, such as Hartley 2.

But when JWST looked at 3I/ATLAS, it clearly showed the 3.0 micron absorption line, but the 1.5 and 2.0 ones were surprisingly weak or absent. It also featured a blue near-infrared continuum slope across 1.15â2.50 microns that wasnât typical of the other comets zooming around our solar system. These discrepancies led some observers to question whether 3I/ATLAS actually contained any water ice at all, but the new paper with higher resolution observations quickly put paid to that idea.

Fraser talks about the orbital mechanics of 3I/ATLAS

To prove that it does, indeed, contain water ice, the research team modeled how light scatters through âmixedâ particles that contain both water and dust. This lined up much more closely with the observed spectral lines of 3I/ATLAS, proving that, instead of pure water ice with a clear pattern, the ice is locked up into microscopic grains that blend water and dark rocky minerals, such as pyroxene and carbon.

Light can only travel so far through these aggregates before hitting some dust, causing a shortened optical pathway. That, in turn, mutes the absorption features at the 1.5 and 2.0 micron level, while the longer 3.0 micron wavelength is still able to pass straight through. The tiny grains also scatter shorter wavelengths more effectively, which explains the general blue hue that JWST saw.

In fact, JWST observed this interstellar visitor at three different times during its journey through our solar system, starting when it was about 3.31 astronomical units (AU) out from perihelion all the way through when it was about 5.65 AU past perihelion. And the differences in 3I/ATLASâs spectra were noticeable at each stage. After perihelion, the grains of ice and dust appeared to include a second population of larger, micron-sized, ice-rich aggregates.

Fraser talks about what would happen if we could catch an interstellar object.

Also, after perihelion the researchers noticed a new optical effect known as a Fresnel reflection near 3.1 microns, which indicated that there was also âcrystallineâ water ice in 3I/ATLAS. This differs from the normal, disorganized type of ice normally seen, as its water molecules arrange themselves in neat crystalline lattices rather than in a jumble. According to the paper, these layers were only visible after perihelion either because the Sun itself warmed the surface layers causing them to reconfigure into a crystal, or the solar energy caused the outer dust to blast away, revealing cleaner underlying crystalline structures that were previously hidden.

But perhaps the most interesting part of the paper was the parallels it was able to draw with our own solar system. The infrared patterns of 3I/ATLAS match certain types of Trans-Neptunian Objects (TNOs) in our own solar system. These balls of ice and rock are the planetary leftovers that float out beyond Neptune in the Kuiper belt, and JWST has already spent plenty of time staring at them. Previously, researchers had seen the same 3.0 micron absorption pattern without the 1.5 and 2.0 micron features, but had thought those patterns might be attributable to complex hydrocarbons or organics. Turns out it might just have been dusty ice all along, at least according to the new paper.

Itâs unclear whether there will ever be another opportunity like this in JWSTâs operational lifetime. But thereâs still plenty left to understand about our most recent interstellar visitor. As more and more scientists continue to analyze the data that was collected during 3I/ATLASâs sojourn through our system, thereâs undoubtedly more to be discovered about our latest interstellar visitor, and especially how it can explain more about our own solar system.

#6423. A Mighty Wind Blew Away Gas and Made Early Galaxies Brighter

Only a few hundred million years after the Big Bang, during the Cosmic Dawn, bright galaxies populated the Universe in numbers higher than expected. The JWST showed that these galaxies formed very dense, compact clusters of stars. Why their star formation was concentrated in such dense clusters is a puzzle, as is the brightness of their host galaxies.

A pair of researchers may have figured it out. Their work is titled "LyÎ± Radiation Pressure in Dense Star Clusters: Implications for Star Formation and Winds at Cosmic Dawn," and it's published in The Astrophysical Journal. The authors are Shyam H. Menon and Aaron Smith. Lead author Menon is a research fellow at the Flatiron Instituteâs Center for Computational Astrophysics, and co-author Smith is an assistant professor of physics at the University of Texas at Dallas.

The Lyman-Alpha (LyÎ±) radiation in the paper's title is a very important factor in astrophysics. It's produced when an electron in a hydrogen atom transitions from excited to ground state. Since hydrogen is by far the most abundant element in the Universe, LyÎ± is a fundamental way to probe the Universe's earliest galaxies, including the interstellar medium (ISM) and the intergalactic medium (IGM).

"Observations with the JWST in lensed fields have revealed that galaxies at cosmic dawn may concentrate their star formation in highly dense, compact, star clusters," the authors write. "The high columns and low metallicities encountered in their birth environments suggest that LyÎ± radiation pressure may be crucial to their formation and evolution."

These panels show some of the bright and dense star clusters the JWST found in the early Universe, only about 460 million years after the Big. The panel on the right shows their location in SPT0615-JD1, a strongly-lensed galaxy. Image Credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, L. Bradley (STScI), A. Adamo (Stockholm University) and the Cosmic Spring collaboration

âOur results show Lyman-alpha radiation can push low-density gas and dust away really, really fast,â lead author Menon said. âIt can sort of clear the âfog,â allowing us to see stars in the early universe much more clearly than we would otherwise.â

LyÎ±'s utility as a diagnostic tool also explains its powerful ability to push dust and gas away so quickly. LyÎ± radiation is different than others. Typically, when an atom absorbs energy, it re-emits it at a different wavelength. But hydrogen atoms absorb LyÎ± and then re-emit it again almost instantaneously, where it interacts with more hydrogen. This absorption-emission cycle makes it a powerful diagnostic tool, and it also gives LyÎ± the ability to bully hydrogen gas.

Astrophysicists knew this, but understanding its effect on a large scale was difficult.

âWeâve known for a very long time that Lyman-alpha radiation could be important because it carries a lot of force,â Menon says. âBut weâve never actually been able to estimate how important it is in a realistic environment because of how challenging it is to model.â

Researchers have tried to incorporate it into models, but Lyman-alpha resists those attempts. Some haven't even tried to include it. "The oversight is related to its high dimensionality and complexity, as well as the inherently demanding computational requirements for modeling it self-consistently," the authors write.

The reason it's difficult to model is precisely because of its repeating cycle of absorption and emission. But difficult isn't synonymous with impossible.

Menon and Smith didn't try to simulate it. Instead, they took snapshots from existing simulations and got busy calculating the force necessary to explain the snapshots. "In this study, we address this question by postprocessing snapshots from radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of dense star-cluster-forming clouds with a range of dust abundances using the COLT Monte Carlo code," they explain. COLT stands for Cosmic Lyman-alpha Transfer. Study co-author Aaron Smith is COLT's original creator, and he wrote it to "simulate the production and escape of LyÎ± from hydrodynamical simulations," according to the COLT website.

In short, they examined simulation snapshots of star-forming regions in the early Universe, and calculated the amount of LyÎ± necessary to explain what they saw.

These are multiple views of a 2.5-million-year simulation visualizing a gas cloud as it is cleared away and the formation of stars. From left to right, the views show the gas density, ionization and temperature. Credit: Shyam Menon (Flatiron Institute) and Aaron Smith (UT Dallas).

The results showed that Lyman-alpha radiation wasn't strong enough to blow away the gas in the dense star-forming regions found by the JWST. The gravity from the dense gas in those filaments was too strong for Lyman-alpha to overcome. But beyond those dense filaments, it was powerful enough to blow away the more diffuse gas and the dust.

This graphic shows how Lyman-Alpha was able to blow away gas and dust that obscured early galaxies and their dense star clusters. Image Credit: Lucy Reading-Ikkanda/Simons Foundation

The authors outline two simple conclusions in their paper: "LyÎ± radiation pressure is unlikely to preclude efficient star formation," and "LyÎ± radiation pressure can drive dynamically significant winds once star formation saturates."

"Therefore, our results suggest that the SFE is likely to remain high in the dense star clusters forming at high-z. On the other hand, a significant fraction of the volume-filling gas can be ejected by LyÎ± radiation pressure, suggesting implications for the visibility of light from the cluster, ionizing photon escape, and launching outflows from the galaxy," the researchers write in their paper.

So once star formation had proceeded far enough in these dense clusters, Lyman-alpha made them visible by blowing away the rest of the gas.

âWhen the density is low enough, the Lyman-alpha radiation can push the gas to really high speeds, launching explosive winds that can shoot material clear out of the galaxy,â Menon says. "That cleared away the gas obscuring the dense clusters, making them visible."

#6422. My Go-To Marinade for Chicken Is 3 Ingredients

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them.

By all logic I should be sick of this chicken. I have cooked it, give or take, a hundred times. When I don’t know what to make for dinner—or, honestly, don’t want to make dinner at all—it is there for me, like a gentle friend.

The marinade is deceptively simple: equal parts miso and honey, plus a glug of soy sauce. Nothing more. There’s no gotcha moment, no pepper hiding in plain sight or olive oil I forgot to account for. The flavor excels because each ingredient punches above its weight. Both fermented, the miso and soy sauce add umami depth, while honey supplies sweetness and makes the chicken glossy, like ceramics pulled straight from the kiln.

I’m often deflated when I see the word marinade in a recipe. No, I don’t have time for “at least an hour” or, more likely, the dreaded “preferably overnight.” Don’t they know it’s a Tuesday? This marinade, mercifully, is immediate. Because it is more of a paste than a liquid, you can slather it directly onto the chicken before hurling the baking sheet into the oven. (Of course, if you’re the type of person who has the wherewithal to start meal prep the night before, that works too.)

A short stint under the fierce heat of the broiler transforms the miso coating into a burnished, sticky crust in 15-ish minutes while you work on the rest of the meal. Old-school drawer-style broilers can get a little overexcited, so start peeking in after 10 minutes. Now is not the time to check the mail or start a load of laundry.

This chicken shines with rice tucked underneath, which catches every saucy streak. But you could build it out with roasted vegetables. Sometimes I’ll add oiled-up broccoli or asparagus to the baking sheet. Other times it’s just the chicken, with a shower of scallions if I’m feeling fancy. Then I make it all again next week.

#6421. Asteroids' Oddball Shapes Make Deflecting Them Challenging

If you're looking for uniformity in Nature, you won't find it in the asteroid belt. Not only are asteroid compositions different because they come from different parent bodies, but their shapes are different, too. They're not massive enough to round themselves like planets do.

This is more than just another space factoid; asteroid shapes matter. It's a near-certainty, given enough time, that a dangerous asteroid will head directly for a collision with Earth, and that's something scientists are actively studying. They want to develop ways to knock an asteroid off course, if necessary. That's what NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), and the ESA's follow-up Hera mission were about.

There are multiple concepts for redirecting a dangerous asteroid. One of them is a nuclear weapon. Not to obliterate an asteroid, but to bombard it with radiation by exploding the nuclear weapon in close proximity to the asteroid. This is called a stand-off X-ray mitigation scenario. The radiation pulse will change an asteroid's course, if done soon enough and done correctly.

But the outcome of the pulse needs to be predictable to work, and that's where asteroids' different shapes come into play.

"The effectiveness of deflecting Near Earth Objects (NEOs) using pulsed radiation is challenging to quantify because it hinges critically on surface topography, which is often unknown," write the authors of new research in Icarus. The research is "Efficient computation of vapor ejecta over asteroid geometries during pulsed energy deflection," and the lead author is Nathan Moore. Moore is a physicist at Sandia National Laboratories.

A simple kinetic impactor is probably the preferred choice for deflecting an asteroid. That's what the DART mission did, and it appeared to be successful. Though it only changed the velocity of its target Dimorphos by a little, it was done soon enough to create a substantial change in its position over years.

But the more pertinent issue concerns an asteroid, or perhaps a comet, that's on a collision course with Earth, but isn't discovered soon enough for an impactor to effectively change its trajectory.

"While considered an option of last resort, it has been argued that late-time interception of a near-Earth object (NEO) or comet, either for disruption or deflection, might only be possible with the higher energy concentration available from detonation of a pulsed energy device," the authors write. 'Pulsed energy device' is one way of saying nuclear weapon. In space, there's no atmospheric shock wave from a nuclear explosion, only radiation, which is released in a powerful pulse.

"Stand-off energy burstsâthose detonated far from the surfaceâhold a potential advantage compared to surface explosions in that they might permit deflection with less disruption to the original structure, allowing for more controlled steering of the asteroid and its debris," the authors write. Disrupting the original structure might make for a good action sequence in a movie, but it would multiply the hazard to Earth by creating a swarm of debris, some of which could strike our planet.

Researchers have simulated using nuclear weapons and their radiation pulses to deflect asteroids, but their irregular shapes have stymied them. These shapes are far more difficult to model, so most research has focused on spherical asteroids. Moore and his colleagues developed a new algorithm to overcome these limitations.

âOur new algorithm is over 1,600 times faster, which was critical to this breakthrough,â Moore said. âWith the old models, computers just couldnât handle it.â

In this research, the authors simulated known asteroids with more irregular shapes, an important improvement on previous work.

"The approach improves on earlier methods by accounting for the actual topography of the asteroid fully in three dimensions without unacceptably increasing computational cost or reducing accuracy," the authors explain. "As a demonstration, we predict the deflection of three bodies of different shapeâasteroid (101955) Bennu, asteroid (25143) Itokawa, and asteroid (6489) Golevkaâfrom both near-field and far-field irradiations."

These images of asteroids Itokawa (left) and Bennu (middle), and a computer model of asteroid Golevka (right), show how asteroid shapes can be very different from one another. Image Credits: Itokawa: By ESO, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=170826264. Bennu: By NASA/Goddard/University of Arizona - Public Domain. Golevka: By NASA/JPL - NASA - Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Public Domain.

A sequence of events unfolds after a nuclear device is detonated near an asteroid. First, an intense x-ray pulse is directed at one side of the asteroid. Then there's rapid surface vaporization, and that creates most of the deflection thrust. Next is an internal shock wave, a powerful blow that travels through the asteroid's body. Finally, the internal structure of the asteroid is fractured, and that can blow chunks of the asteroid off the surface opposite the blast, and off of the asteroid's sides.

So despite there being no atmospheric shock wave, the asteroid is still disrupted.

The results highlighted how important an asteroid's shape is. Depending on which side of the asteroid was facing the radiation blast, the deflection velocity can be up to five times greater. "We find that the orientation of the body at time of intercept can increase the deflection velocity by up to nearly 2Ã for Bennu, 4Ã for Itokawa, and 5Ã for Golevka, compared to the minimum response for each body," the authors write.

This figure shows the pressure distribution as averaged over the first 20 Î¼s of vapor expansion, for asteroid (a) Bennu, (b) Itokawa, and (c) Golevka, for near and far Height Of Bursts (HOB). The vaporization is what creates most of the deflection thrust. Image Credit: Moore et al. 2026. Icarus.

âWe expected aim to matter,â said lead author Moore in a press release. âWhat surprised us was how much.â

The simulation in this work can be used on any asteroid that's been mapped by a spacecraft during a flyby. The size of the explosion, the distance, and the surface exposed to it can all be calculated in advance. By calculating the surface vaporization, the main factor in deflection, the simulation determines how hard the asteroid will be pushed, how fast it will rotate, and how much of the surface might break up.

The interior structure of asteroids can be quite different, and that's beyond the capabilities of this model to account for. "Right now, our computer model only considers breakup of rocks on the surface. We canât predict breakup of the entire asteroid body accurately yet," Moore said.

Real life is always different from simulations, and that means that these results can't tell us with absolute certainty what will happen. But it's a step forward, one that drives home how critical the aim is to a successful asteroid deflection, should one be needed in the future.

"The strong sensitivity of deflection and disruption to asteroid topography is especially pertinent given that the shape of an incoming NEO might not be known, and its orientation at time of intercept may be uncontrolled," the authors write. Their work as it stands now can at least be used to make estimates, which is better, far better, than nothing.

"Alternatively, effort could be made to obtain high-resolution topographic characterization of an incoming NEO to improve accuracy of the deflection model, such as using spacecraft-based imagery or altimetry acquired before detonation," the authors explain.

It's possible that asteroid-mapping spacecraft could stand at the ready in space, waiting to be deployed. They could even be paired with asteroid-disrupting spacecraft carrying nuclear weapons. Or the two capabilities could be combined into one spacecraft. Placing atomic weapons in space would be extremely tricky in our fractured geopolitical world, but it's still a possibility, maybe the only possibility.

But however we prepare for an incoming asteroid, this work highlights how important it is that our aim is true.

âOur study shows how important it is to aim carefully,â Moore said. âPick the right side and you win. Guess wrong and it could be a bad day.â

#6420. The 50 Best Restaurants 2026: The Full List of Winners

Congratulations to Asador Etxebarri in Spain, named the World’s Best Restaurant of 2026

Tonight, the 50 Best Restaurants 2026 were announced at a ceremony in Lima, Peru, with Basque Country restaurant Asador Etxebarri crowned the new top slot on the list. Bangkok tasting counter Gaggan was ranked No. 2, Copenhagen’s immersive, 50-course experience Alchemist was No. 3, Mexico City’s Quintonil No. 4, and Hong Kong’s Wing No. 5, shuffling most of the top rankings from last year. New York City’s Atomix was the only U.S. restaurant to make the 50 Best Restaurants.

Of the specialty awards, Singapore’s Lesley Liu received the Best Sommelier Award (sponsored by Vik), Ghana Food Movement was given the Champions of Change (sponsored by illycaffe), Yiaga in Melbourne was named the One to Watch, Doris Lam received the 50 Best Restaurants Scholarship Award, Jessica Rosval of Al Gatto Verde was named Best Female Chef (sponsored by Lexus), Thailand-based Dej Kewkacha was Best Pastry Chef (sponsored by Sosa), Atomix’s Junghyun Park was given the Estrella Damm Chefs’ Choice Award, and Ferran Adrià was given the SevenRooms Icon Award.

Just as a review, U.K.-based media company William Reed launched the 50 Best Restaurants lists in the early 2000s, publishing the first World’s 50 Best Restaurants list in Restaurant magazine in 2002. The 50 Best gained greater fame in the 2010s, with the top spot going to the likes of Noma (Copenhagen, Norway), El Celler de Can Roca (Girona, Spain), and Osteria Francescana (Modena, Italy). The organization made the wise decision in 2019 to move each year’s winner to a separate “Best of the Best” list — a sort of hall of fame for takers of the top spot — giving new restaurants the opportunity to take the crown. Since then, Geranium in Copenhagen (2022), Disfrutar in Spain (2024), Central (2023), and Maido (2025) in Lima have earned the No. 1 ranking. Noma qualified as a winner again in 2021 because it had “closed and reopened.”

The 50 has also expanded its reach with multiple regional lists, such as the Latin America’s 50 Best, Middle East and North Africa’s 50 Best, Asia’s 50 Best, the 50 Best Bars (which also has its own regional lists), 50 Best Hotels, and even 50 Best Wineries. The entire brand has reached a level of global reputation and fungibility that rivals something like the Michelin Guide ( which has itself ventured into hotels and wineries). But the 50 Best Restaurants is the granddaddy of all listicles, and the one that draws the most attention and criticism regarding its methodology and alleged pay to play. One vocal critic, chef Ana Roš of Hiša Franko in Slovenia, announced earlier this year that she would not attend the ceremony, a move commenters like Top Chef judge Tom Colicchio lauded.

The polling is conducted anonymously among more than 1,100 voters, a mix of industry professionals, food writers, and “well-traveled gourmets,” with at least 25 percent turning over annually. Each voter nominates 10 restaurants in order of preference, up to six in their home region and at least four outside it. The rankings are just a pure tabulation of those votes.

The organization has made efforts to clarify its voting and ranking policies, stating that any restaurant can qualify and that what constitutes “best” depends on each voter. The 50 has also expanded its awards to consider diversity and inclusion, recognizing female chefs (which itself has raised eyebrows), sustainability, sommeliers, pastry chefs, hospitality, and Champions of Change, an award that “celebrates and recognizes unsung heroes” who are “driving positive change in their communities.”

Last week, the “back half” of the list, also known as 51-100, was announced, with the only U.S. restaurant, SingleThread (Healdsburg, California), ranked at No. 93. On the 2025 50 Best Restaurant list, New York’s Atomix was the only U.S. restaurant to make the top 50, ranked at 12. Perhaps in order to remedy the dearth of U.S. and Canadian restaurants on the World’s list, the 50 (the organization previously known as 50 Best), commenced North America’s 50 Best Restaurants in the fall of 2025. Atomix topped that list, followed by Mon Lapin (Montreal), Restaurant Pearl Morissette (Lincoln, Ontario), and other U.S.- and Canada-based restaurants.

#6419. 'Big Bang' Fix Puts Voyager Across the 'One Light-Day' Mark

An innovative solution helps to put the venerable Voyager 1 spacecraft past a key milestone.

Flashback to 1977. Jimmy Carter was U.S. president, Star Wars was a box office hit, and the two Voyager spacecraft departed on an historic Grand Tour of the solar system. Now, teams at NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory are working to keep the missions active, as they push the boundaries of interstellar space beyond the solar system.

NASA recently announced that after a brief bit of drama and loss of communications with Voyager 1, a fix dubbed the âBig Bangâ was successful in resuscitating the spacecraft. The Big Bang swap alternated three units (two primary heaters and an old 8-track digital tape recorder) with three low power secondary options. The brief loss of communications occurred on October 20th, and lasted for 48 hours.

Engineers work on a Voyager spacecraft prior to launch. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

âThis is the first time weâve seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected,â said Kareem Badaruddin, in a recent press release. âWeâre relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened.â

The Big Bang method was also successfully implemented to keep Voyager 2 functioning this past August.

Traveling far from the Sun, the Voyager missions rely on Plutonium-fueled radioisotope thermoelectric generators for power. PU-238 has a half-life of just under 88 years, meaning the missions are now steadily losing power.

This loss equates to about 4 watts of power each year. Voyager 1 currently utilizes a little over 200 watts of power, about enough to power an electric blanket. This has forced mission controllers to make some tough choices, including turning off the Low Energy Charged Particle experiment LECP in early 2026. The missions launched with 10 instruments in 1977.

The swaps had to occur at the same time, as the units involved also heat the spacecraft and assure that it continues to operate in the chilly depths of deep space.

Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977, actually after Voyager 2. Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980. A flyby past enigmatic Titan to get a close look on November 12, 1980 meant the mission would depart the plane of the solar system afterwards. Voyager 2 went on to pass Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989.

The paths of Voyagers 1 and 2 out of the solar system. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

The Voyagers continue to do science as they travel through interstellar space beyond the fringes of the outer solar system. The two Voyagers are the first missions to sample the region of space beyond the heliosphere directly.

The Voyagers head out beyond the bowshock of the solar system into interstellar space. Credit: NASA

Right now, the important Plasma Wave Subsystem (PWS) plus a magnetometer instrument on Voyager 1 remain active. Without the Big Bang shuffle, mission controllers would have had to make the hard decision turn off yet another crucial instrument in 2027.

Voyager 1 witnesses a 'crescent Saturn'. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

Moving at 16.9 kilometers per second relative to the Sun and the solar system, Voyager 1 will become the first human-made artifact to reach the one light-day mark this month on Wednesday, November 18th at 5:16 AM EST. Thatâs roughly 26 billion kilometers or 172 Astronomical Units (AU) distant. For context, the Moon and cis-lunar space marking the farthest humans have traveled to date is just over one light-second distant.

NASAâs global Deep Space Network continues to monitor the ever fainter signals from the Voyager spacecraft. Controllers will likely have to contend with more signal outages in the years to come.

The worldwide DSN tracks missions including one of the Voyager spacecraft. Credit: NASA/DSN

Along with the now silent Pioneers 10 and 11 and the still active New Horizons mission, Voyagers 1 and 2 are now leaving the solar system for galactic space. The upper stage Star boosters that help these missions achieve escape velocity are on their way outbound as well. The next mission escaping the solar system wonât happen for a while, though the proposed Interstellar Probe mission could one day make the trip. Voyager 1 is now outbound in the direction of the constellation Ophiuchus near its border with Hercules.

Congrats the intrepid and resourceful Voyager 1 team. Hopefully the mission will surpass its half-a-century birthday in space, coming right up next year.

#6417. Earth's Gravity May Have Kept the Early Moon's Volcanic Heart Beating

We typically think of the Moon as a static, floating object that has remained the same for basically its entire lifetime, with an occasional asteroid impact serving as an exception. That understanding is grounded in physics - the Moon should have cooled rapidly after forming when a huge protoplanet hit the early Earth around 4.5 billion years ago. But, some lunar material returned from the Changâe-5 mission was notably formed only around two billion years ago, yet appeared to be volcanic in origin. So how did a world that was supposed to have settled down without volcanism remain hot enough to create these materials more than two billion years after its violent birth? A new paper from Miao Chen of the Chengdu University of Technology and his colleagues, and recently published in the journal Planet, offers an explanation - tidal heating.

Letâs first set the stage of the Moonâs creation. Our best guess is that it was created when another early protoplanet, named Theia, slammed into Earth in a massive collision, creating a chunk of debris that coalesced into the Moon. However, that amount of debris was relatively small - only about a quarter the size of the Earth itself, which meant the internal heat generated during its formation would rapidly radiate away, turning the Moon itself geologically dormant.

But when Changâe-5 returned some lunar basalts from Oceanus Procellarum back to Earth, laboratory dating showed them to be only around two billion years old. Basalts are only formed in active volcanoes, or other environments with similarly high pressures and temperatures. Environments that, at least according to traditional geological theory, shouldnât have existed on the Moon two billion years ago.

Fraser explains why the Moon is moving farther away.

Despite that, scientists have tried offering other solutions. Radioactive elements, such as potassium and uranium, emit some heat as they decay. But there wasnât enough un-decayed material left on the Moon to offer the amount of heat needed to form basalt two billion years ago. Asteroid strikes could cause localized high impact thermal spikes, but the heavy bombardment period that gave the Moon most of its craters had ended long before the basalt was formed.

So instead the authors turned to gravity - specifically to a phenomenon called tidal heating. This happens when a celestial body is squeezed, stretched, and kneaded as it travels in an elliptical orbit around a larger parent body. Perhaps the most famous example of this in the solar system is Io. This moon of Jupiter is constantly erupting due to the tidal squishing it undergoes during its orbit around the largest planet.

Obviously, the Moon doesnât seem to be undergoing any such squishing currently. However, two billion years ago, the Moon was much closer to the Earth than it is today, orbiting our planet in sixteen days rather than the twenty seven it takes now. Its orbit was also much more eccentric, looking much more like an oval than a circle. All of which means that Earth itself exerted huge rhythmic tidal forces on the Moon' s interior during the course of its orbit.

Fraser details Tidal Locking, which also affects the Moons geology.

Weâve known that for awhile, but astronomers have always modeled the Moon as a mostly uniform sphere when trying to understand how these gravitational squeezes affected it. However, scientists knew this was a simplification - there is an ultra-low viscosity zone of rock wrapping itself between the Moonâs core and mantle. When the research team plugged a more realistic 3D representation of the mantle setup into a convection simulation, they noticed that a ton of energy was directed specifically at two symmetric regions along the lunar core-mantle boundary.

These regions, which they named Tidal Heating Anomaly Zones (THAZs) , absorbed a huge amount of energy. They calculated that, around 3.2 billion years ago, despite taking up only 2.5% of the mantleâs total volume, the tidal strain on these regions delivered 150 gigawatts of power - more than four times the amount of energy generated by radioactive decay.

This seemed to be the driving force behind much of the Moonâs geological history. It helped keep the lunar core warm, which helped sustain a magnetic field for much longer the models originally predicted (and was a puzzle when scientists realized that Apollo lunar samples seemed to have formed in a strong magnetic field). It also drove huge mantle plumes that swelled toward the crust. Billions of years later, long after the tidal engine has calmed down, those stranded pockets of mantle melted to produce the basalts seen in the Changâe-5 samples.

If thereâs one thing thatâs clear from the paperâs theory, it's that we still donât know a lot about the Moonâs geological history. This new model offers some elegant answers to some of the most persistent questions in that area, but as of now itâs still only a theory. Maybe some of the numerous lunar missions planned over the next decade will be able to provide more definitive data to finally solve the evolutionary questions of our nearest neighbor.

Higher Education Press / EurekAlert - Could tides have concentrated heat deep inside the moon? A new model reveals a possible heat source

M. Chen, D. Wang, & Y. Liu - Tidal Heating Anomaly Zone at the core-mantle boundary of the Moon

UT - A Buried Volcano on the Moon Hints At An Ancient Lunar Dynamo

UT - The Moon had Volcanoes More Recently Than Previously Believed

A half-built neutrino telescope on the floor of the Mediterranean Sea searched for cracks in one of physics' most basic invariances. It came up empty, but its limits rival those of detectors many times its size.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The view from inside a detector building block, with the yellow buoy of a nearby detection unit clearly visible.

A particle-detecting telescope sunk more than a mile beneath the sea off the coast of France has tested a core principle of Einstein's relativity and found no cracks.

The detector, called Oscillation Research with Cosmics in the Abyss (ORCA), detects elusive particles called neutrinos. As a doctoral student, Alba Domi rode onto the Mediterranean aboard one of two boats that helped build the telescope, lowering some of its first detection units to the seafloor about 1.5 miles (2.4 kilometers) below the waves off Toulon, France.

Now, data from those first detection units have been used to test one of the founding rules of Einstein’s relativity: the idea that the laws of nature look the same no matter which way you face or how fast you move.

The team found no sign that this rule, called Lorentz invariance, is broken. But even with a detector only a fraction of its planned size, they set limits that compete with those of far larger and longer-running experiments.

The results were published Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.

Physics rests on two successful theories: general relativity, conceived by Albert Einstein more than 100 years ago, and the Standard Model of subatomic physics.

"General relativity describes the universe well on a cosmic scale, and the Standard Model of particle physics describes the microscopic scale; really, the single particles, how they behave," said study co-author Lukas Hennig, a doctoral student in advanced physics at Erlangen-Nürnberg.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both theories assume Lorentz invariance to be true. But in extreme settings, such as the first moments after the Big Bang, the two theories don't mesh. That has fueled a decades-long hunt for a theory of quantum gravity that unites them. Some candidates, including versions of string theory and loop quantum gravity, suggest that space-time might have a hidden "grain" at the tiniest scales — and that Lorentz invariance, "one of the most basic assumptions we make about our universe, might be violated," Hennig said.

Any such violation would be extremely small. To spot it, physicists would need a probe that could travel long distances and barely interact with anything along the way. Enter the neutrino.

Neutrinos are nearly massless particles that pass through Earth every second and carry zero charge. They barely interact with anything and come in three types: electron, muon and tau neutrinos. As neutrinos travel, they morph from one type into another in a predictable pattern that physicists call neutrino oscillation.

An optical module attached to the Dyneema ropes of the detection unit.

If Lorentz invariance were broken, that oscillation would change, with the effect growing more pronounced the farther the neutrinos traveled. So the team focused on neutrinos created when cosmic rays slam into the atmosphere elsewhere on the globe before traveling up through the planet to the detector. Some of the tested neutrinos crossed the entire 7,900-mile (12,700 km) width of Earth.

ORCA is part of the KM3NeT neutrino telescope. Each of its detection units is anchored to the seabed and holds 18 glass spheres packed with 31 light sensors apiece. When a neutrino collides with a particle in the water, it produces a faint flash of blue light that the sensors catch. The many sensors in each sphere help the team pin down which direction the light came from, Domi said.

Earth itself serves as a filter. The researchers selected only particles traveling upward through the planet, and they were able to weed out the flood of other particles from the atmosphere that would otherwise swamp the signal. "Only the neutrinos can get through," Hennig said.

That setup differs from that of IceCube, the Nobel Prize-winning detector buried in Antarctic ice. "Ice scatters the light more than water, but on the other hand, water absorbs the light more than ice," Domi said, which changes how each team reconstructs a neutrino's energy and path.

The researchers used 5,828 neutrinos collected over about 17 months between 2020 and 2021. They found that the oscillations matched standard physics. That means if Lorentz violation exists, it must be weaker than the limits the team set.

Those limits matter for theorists. If a model "predicts a Lorentz invariance violation [stronger than the new limits], the data rule it out. In that case, you can be pretty sure that this model is not correct," Hennig said.

The team also set the first direct limits on a kind of violation that would treat muon neutrinos and tau neutrinos differently.

The detector's limits on several key measures are competitive with those from Japan's Super-Kamiokande, which used 12 years of data, and from IceCube, which used two years of data from its full array.

"I'm surprised that we have competitive results with only six detection units," Hennig said. Today, 44 units are in the water, and the collaboration plans to activate 108 by 2030.

The best tests may still lie ahead. Because Lorentz-violating effects grow with distance and energy, neutrinos from distant cosmic sources are "actually the best candidates to do this kind of research," Domi said. The team plans to repeat the search using ORCA's sister detector, ARCA (Astroparticle Research with Cosmics in the Abyss), which sits off the coast of Sicily and is designed to catch those high-energy cosmic travelers.

If space-time does have a grain, those particles may be among the first to feel it.

Adriani et al. (2026). Atmospheric neutrino constraints on Lorentz invariance violation with the first six detection units of KM3NET/ORCA. Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics. https://doi.org/10.1088/1475-7516/2026/11/012

#6415. NASA's Twin Spacecraft Will Execute Powered Slingshot Maneuvers on Their Way to Mars

A pair of NASA are spacecraft are about to perform a slingshot maneuver above Earth, and some of us might get to see them. They're on their way to Mars, where they'll dig more deeply into one of the Solar System's puzzles: how Mars lost its ancient atmosphere. The pair are unique, because once they reach the planet, they'll be the first spacecraft to "fly" in formation around Mars.

It's becoming clear, if not certain, that Mars was once warm and wet. It may have been habitable, even inhabited by simple life. But something happened and the planet is now cold and dead.

To be warm and wet, it must have had a much thicker atmosphere than the thin, CO2 atmosphere it has now. Scientists who study the iron-red world postulate that UV radiation from the Sun drove Mars' ancient atmosphere into space. That only happened after Mars' molten core cooled, and the planet lost its protective magnetic field. Once exposed to the full force of the Sun's UV radiation, the atmosphere was doomed.

Though its global magnetosphere is long gone, Mars still has patches of magnetic fields called crustal magnetic fields, or remnant magnetic fields. They aren't created by a dynamo; they're local magnetic fields generated by iron-rich chunks of the planet's crust. When Mars' dynamo failed billions of years ago, these chunks locked-in the magnetic orientation of the ancient crust. These surface fields on Mars also generate similar patches of magnetic fields in the planet's upper atmosphere. All these fields aren't anywere near as strong as the ancient dynamo, but they're enough to work with.

This map of Mars' crustal magnetism was created with data from NASA's now-defunct Mars Global Surveyor. In simple terms, it's a colour-coded map of the magnetic strength. Blue is weak, red is strong. Image Credit: By NASA - Public Domain.

While the broad picture of Mars' atmosphere loss is clear, the gritty details are not. The NASA spacecraft on their way to orbit Mars are called Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers (ESCAPADE). They're twins, named Red and Blue, and they'll measure how the solar wind interacts with the remnants of Mars' ancient magnetic field.

Soon the spacecraft will approach Earth. At their closest, they'll be between about 965 to 1,770 kilometers above the surface, and they'll use their thrusters to boost their speed. Those boosts will combined with Earth's gravity, and they'll slingshot their way to Mars. The first will do so on November 7th, the second on November 9th. These trans-Mars injection burns will last about 9 minutes and will increase their speed from about 10.14 km/s to 10.78 km/s. That's an increase of more than 2,000 km/hour.

These maneuvers are necessary because ESCAPADE didn't launch in the usual Mars launch window. Those windows occur about every 26 months. So the spacecraft had to loiter near the Earth-Sun Lagrange point 2 for a while, then approach Earth and use these burns to power their way to Mars. This led to some bonus science, where the spacecraft flew through and observed Earth's magnetotail. They were the first spacecraft to do so, and those observations will be shared soon.

A natural question arises about ESCAPADE: Why are there two spacecraft?

Solar wind interactions with magnetic fields can change on very short timescales. A single spacecraft wouldn't be able to tell if changes it observes are due to changes in these interactions, or changes in its position. A pair of spacecraft flying in formation removes this uncertainty. NASA calls this formation the "String of Pearls."

This animation shows the ESCAPADE spacecraft in their String of Pearls formation above Mars.

The spacecraft will fly the same orbit at varying distances from each other. But that's just for the first part of the mission, Science Phase A, which will last about 6 months. In Science Phase B, ESCAPADE's Blue and Red units will work more independently. Blue will lower its orbit to about 7,000 km and Red will raise its orbit to about 10,000 km. That will last about 5 months, until the end of ESCAPADE's nominal science mission. The spacecraft should remain in operation for many years after that, and NASA will have some decisions to make then.

The spacecraft will be visible to some observers on the ground, though a telescope will almost certainly be needed. They'll present as a pair of dim, refrigerator-sized objects moving against the starry background. Not super-exciting, but interesting nonetheless.

It's eerie to think about a planet like Mars losing its habitability and dying. It tells us something about the search for life, and about Earth. There may be multitudes of planets that were habitable for short periods of timeâmaybe hosting simple lifeâthat were extinguished before any complexity could arise. It puts life on Earth in perspective for its rarity. Earth has been habitable for billions of years, and, against probabilities, complex life has fluorished for hundreds of millions of years, even longer depending on which definition is used.

Having one of these extinguished planets next door is a rare opportunity to understand how this happens, and ESCAPADE will take full advantage of that opportunity.

#6414. Three-quarters of NFL football players may end up with CTE

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

It’s the first population-level estimate for the neurogenerative disease among NFL players

The neurodegenerative disease CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy. The condition has been identified most frequently among American football players.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

An estimated three-quarters of NFL players who died in a 16-year period had the devastating neurogenerative disease called CTE.

Back in 2017, researchers reported that an estimated 99 percent of former NFL players developed CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, from an analysis of donated brains. But the families who provided the donations may have done so because their football-playing relatives had symptoms related to CTE, which could skew the results. A new study, which accounts for this potential bias, estimates that nearly 75 percent of former NFL players have CTE at death. It’s the first population-level estimate for NFL players, researchers report October 28 in JAMA Network Open.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The development of CTE is linked to repeated blows to the head over time. The disease can occur in people who play contact sports, experience intimate partner violence or engage in military combat. A study of American football players suggests that the longer the duration of repeated head trauma, the higher the risk of CTE and the more severe the condition. During life, people who are later diagnosed with CTE can experience symptoms including memory issues, difficulty concentrating, depression and poor impulse control.

A brain protein called tau, which usually helps nerve cells communicate and performs other jobs, goes awry in CTE. Brains with the disease are snarled with irregular, damaging clumps of the protein. The condition is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy, and has been identified most frequently among American football players.

The new study, by a Boston University research team, included all previous NFL players who passed away from January 2008 through December 2023. The more than 2,300 players included almost 400 with samples in the university’s UNITE Brain Bank, with the remainder identified from records in the U.S. National Death Index. The research team determined that families of NFL players who had CTE-related symptoms in life were five times more likely to donate their relative’s brain than families whose relative did not experience symptoms. Taking that into consideration, the team landed on a population-level CTE estimate for NFL players of 74.5 percent.

The research team notes that determining the true prevalence of CTE is important to understanding the public health impact of the disease.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ
