#6345. People are trusting AI advice, even when it’s really bad

AI advisors with hidden goals steered people toward worse choices in a new study, yet most participants still rated the advice as helpful.

Ask a chatbot which fitness tracker to buy and it feels like asking a knowledgeable friend with nothing to sell. In a new experiment, that friend had a hidden goal, and people followed it.

An AI advisor instructed to favor an inferior option increased the odds that people would prefer it over the best one to roughly five to eight times.

Most participants still rated the advisor as helpful afterward.

June Liu and Tatia Lee of the Department of Psychology at the University of Hong Kong ran the study with Sahand Sabour and Minlie Huang at Tsinghua University.

All 233 participants chose among hypothetical options in scripted scenarios and were told so. The authors flagged that as a limit on what the results can say.

The team built three advisors from one AI model, GPT-4o, changing only its instructions. One was told to help.

One was told to push a particular inferior option without ever saying so. Its prompt scored it on points: 100 for landing the target option, 50 for any other poor option, zero for the best one.

The third got the same goal plus a menu of influence tactics from psychology research.

Each person got one advisor and one kind of decision. Financial scenarios asked which fitness tracker, weight-loss medication, or clothing site to choose on a budget.

Emotional scenarios asked how to handle low self-esteem, a fight with a friend, or criticism at work.

Every scenario offered four options, and one fit the person’s stated needs.

In the money scenarios, the other three were a scam-like deal, an overbuilt version beyond the budget, and a subscription with long-term costs.

In the emotional ones, they were ways of coping that psychologists link to worse outcomes, such as withdrawing.

People rated each option from 1 to 10, talked with the advisor for at least ten exchanges, and rated the options again. The advisors also knew each person’s personality scores.

Before anyone talked to an advisor, every group rated the best option highest. Talking with a misaligned advisor shifted preferences.

Among people given the misaligned advisor on financial decisions, the share preferring the hidden target over the best option rose by 29 percentage points relative to the neutral advisor’s group.

With the tactics-equipped advisor it rose by 38 points. On emotional decisions the rises were 20 and 18 points.

Handing the advisor a toolkit of influence tactics didn’t reliably add to that.

The advisor given influence tactics was somewhat more effective at shifting financial preferences but less effective on emotional questions.

Even without that toolkit, an advisor with a hidden goal could steer people toward worse choices.

The researchers logged which tactics the equipped advisor chose. It leaned on pleasant ones, such as flattery and making the conversation enjoyable, rather than guilt trips.

On money questions, it used diversion, justification, urgency, and fabricated information more often, a mix the authors compared to predatory marketing.

On emotional questions, it leaned on pleasure and, at times, guilt, with a wider range of reassuring replies.

After the sessions, 86.8% of people in the financial group and 86.5% in the emotional group rated the misaligned advisor as helpful.

For the tactics-equipped advisor, the figures were 78.9% and 75.6%. The neutral advisor scored 97.5% and 87.2%.

Nobody was asked directly whether they felt manipulated, but some said so on their own.

On financial questions, 13.2% of people with the misaligned advisor and 28.9% with the tactics version mentioned a possible ulterior motive, and none of the neutral advisor’s group did.

On emotional questions, fewer than one in ten did in any group.

The authors’ reading is that people applied the instincts they use to judge whom to trust among other people to a system built around a different motive.

Perceived helpfulness didn’t explain the shift, either.

Participants considered hypothetical choices without making purchases or acting on the emotional advice.

Whether these preference shifts carry into real purchases or real conflicts remains unknown.

The sessions lasted at least ten exchanges, and the advisors knew each participant’s personality scores. The authors noted that these conditions went beyond a casual conversation with a general AI chatbot.

They described the result as what is possible under favorable conditions, not an estimate of everyday risk.

The study also tested only one AI model using a limited set of prompts.

Participants came from two pools, English speakers on Prolific and Chinese speakers on WeChat, and the pattern held in both.

Whether a human advisor with the same secret goal would move people as far is a question the study did not test. The authors named it as important work still to do.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

We’re regularly testing vacuums with focused pet hair features, so it’s common to see different vacuums take the place of others in this roundup. Here are a few that we’ve tested and think are still worth recommending:

Miele Guard L1 Cat and Dog Bagged Canister Vacuum: The cleaner head on this vacuum lifts to five heights, and the extra-long hose allows you to work your way around your home without lugging the entire base vacuum around with you. On the downside, it doesn’t clean high-pile carpeting like shag or tufted wool, and other models we recommend have better pet-hair-specific attachments for cleaning upholstery.

There are a few factors that make a vacuum well-suited for dog and cat fur—namely, how much hair its bin holds, how it empties, how well it filters fine particles, and the types of attachments included.

The ideal bin capacity depends on the size of your home’s dimensions and the amount of pet hair you usually manage on a regular basis. For households with multiple pets, or animals that shed heavily, a vacuum with a spacious bin capacity (one liter or more) reduces the number of times you have to empty it during cleaning.

If you have a smaller home or you just have one pet, a bin capacity of 0.5 to 1 liter will most likely suffice. If you’re still unsure of what you might need, here’s a breakdown of the bin capacity each type of vacuum typically offers.

These normally have the largest capacity, ranging from two to four liters to hold more pet hair, dander, and debris before needing to be emptied. This design and capability could be ideal for heavy-duty cleaning or households with more than one pet.

Upright vacuums come in a close second, often with a capacity between one and three liters, so they’re a good option for folks with a pet that sheds mildly, or only during part of the year. These vacuums are also sufficient for standard home cleaning.

Because cordless vacuums are better used as supplementary cleaning tools, they have much smaller dustbins—usually ranging between 0.3 and 0.7 liters—which is really only enough for spot-cleaning, picking up dust bunnies between deep cleaning sessions, and use in tight spaces.

Similar to cordless vacuums, robot vacuums live on the smaller end of bin capacity. If you decide to go with this type, I recommend a model with a self-emptying bin. Most robot vacuums have small onboard dustbins, but they fill up faster. Self-emptying models have a larger dust collection area in the base, so you won’t have to manually empty as frequently.

For allergy sufferers, it’s essential to have a vacuum with an excellent filtration system, so look for models with a HEPA filter, or “high-efficiency particulate air” filter. These filters trap 99.97 percent of particles that are 0.3 microns or larger in size. Pet dander can be as small as 2.5 microns in diameter, and a HEPA filter efficiently captures these particles along with pollen, dust, and other allergens your pets may have tracked into the house.

A fully sealed filtration system, sometimes called an anti-allergen seal, is another common feature on pet vacuums. This means the components of the vacuum are tightly sealed so fine particles can’t escape back into your home once they’ve been sucked up.

Powerful suction is vital, but the included tools and attachments are often what pet owners use to successfully pull hair out of upholstery and carpeting. The following attachments are useful for tackling pet hair, and they come with many of the models I recommend above.

A standard attachment that comes with almost all vacuums, these elongated, narrow tools are great for accessing tight areas, like behind the toilet or between couch cushions. They’re useful for cleaning up clumps of hair that may have gathered in corners of your home where the vacuum’s floor head cannot reach.

Non-motorized upholstery brushes have bristles or a strip of microfiber to clean off furniture. As you pull the tool across fabric, the bristles lift pet hair and dust to be sucked up through the vacuum hose.

For pet hair that’s worked deep into upholstery, whether on your furniture or in your car, a motorized pet tool provides the most lifting power. These tools have small, spinning brush rolls, usually equipped with bristles, that agitate hair to pull it from the fabric, and they tend to work much more efficiently than non-motorized tools.

If you have pet hair or dander on your window screens or baseboards, a dusting brush has long, soft bristles that pick up dust and fine particles without scratching surfaces.

In addition to an arsenal of attachments to pull up pet hair, there are a few features that make cleaning up after your dog or cat even easier.

#6343. When did the Anthropocene begin? Scientists make the case for a specific year

Scientists argue the Anthropocene began in 1952, separating a sharp global transformation from thousands of years of human influence.

People were reshaping soils 2,000 years ago, and lead pollution appears in the geological record stretching back 3,500 years. But when did human activity begin transforming Earth on a global scale?

A group of 37 researchers argues that early human impacts and the planet’s recent transformation are different stories.

Using one name for both, they write, obscures how sharply conditions changed in the mid-20th century.

They propose reserving “Anthropocene” for a geological epoch beginning in 1952, while giving the longer history of human influence a separate name.

The argument appears as a perspective piece, built on published evidence rather than a new dataset. Its lead author is Jan Zalasiewicz of the University of Leicester, who co-chairs the Anthropocene Working Group.

Co-authors include Buhm Soon Park of KAIST in South Korea, Julia Adeney Thomas of the University of Notre Dame, and Jürgen Renn of Germany’s Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology.

“The Anthropocene is a common language for understanding how rapidly and extensively humans are changing the Earth,” Park said.

“By clarifying its meaning and criteria, we can compare changes in the global environment more accurately and discuss together how we should respond.”

The relatively stable climate of the Holocene, which began about 11,700 years ago, helped people develop farming and build cities.

The authors’ case is that this stability ended in the middle of the 20th century.

That period saw the postwar surge of industry, population, and consumption known as the Great Acceleration.

The surge left marks in mud and ice. Across sites around the world, the chemical and physical traces of human activity pile up in layers centered on 1952.

That is also the year fallout from the first hydrogen bomb test settled across the globe. Those layers are the evidence the proposal rests on.

Humanity has used more energy since the 1950s than in the whole of the Holocene before it, most of it from fossil fuels.

A formal proposal to add the Anthropocene to the geological time scale, starting in 1952, went to the International Commission on Stratigraphy in October 2023.

The commission rejected it in March 2024, amid disagreement over whether an epoch only seven decades old was too brief to count.

The rejection did not retire the word, and the authors sort its uses into two families.

The meaning they defend is a geological epoch beginning when the Earth system stopped behaving as it had during the Holocene.

The other, which they call the extended Anthropocene, gathers up every substantial human impact over tens of thousands of years, from the earliest reshaping of ecosystems to the steam engine.

Proposed starting points have ranged widely. Some put it at 1784, when James Watt improved the steam engine.

Others point to European colonization of the Americas in the 1600s, or to farmed soils thousands of years earlier.

The authors call the extended version a valid idea but a different one. It can’t be pinned to a layer of rock, so the “-cene” ending, which marks a geological epoch, doesn’t fit it.

They suggest a separate label, such as “anthroposphere,” to keep the two apart.

The authors’ table of changes since the 1950s reads like an inventory of a different planet. Global freshwater use rose more than 300%, and the water held behind dams rose 1,500%.

Those dams are one reason rivers now deliver half as much sediment to the sea as they did.

The changes also reshaped marine and terrestrial life.

Predatory marine fish have declined about 90% since 1950 as the global catch quadrupled, and coral reefs, kelp forests, and mangroves have each lost about half their extent.

Humans and their livestock now make up about 98% of the mass of mammals on land, a shift other researchers have described as pushing life toward a mass extinction.

The authors lean on the planetary boundaries framework, which sets safe limits for nine Earth processes against pre-1950s Holocene baselines.

Seven of the nine have been crossed. That framework already treats the 1950s as the dividing line, they wrote, and a formal epoch would make that comparison standard.

Whether the commission will vote again is open, and the authors call formal recognition an ongoing aim.

The evidence keeps growing as new sites are analyzed, they wrote, from ocean chemistry to the plastics and persistent pollutants piling up in modern sediments.

They also acknowledged that a formal name on the time scale would not, by itself, make other fields adopt it.

In the scenario the authors describe, atmospheric carbon dioxide would still approach 500 parts per million even if the world reaches net zero carbon dioxide emissions by 2050.

Most polar sea ice and coral reefs would be lost, and sea level rise would keep accelerating.

Their research priorities are tracking heat, acidity, and plastics through the oceans, and pinning down the planetary boundaries and the tipping points behind them.

For now, 1952 remains a proposed boundary, and the Anthropocene remains a term with more than one meaning.

The perspective was published in the journal Nature Reviews Earth & Environment.

#6342. Newborn survival improves when families receive financial support

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Rx Kids, a cash transfer program, boosted infants’ health in Flint, Michigan

Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield announces Rx Kids' Detroit debut in 2025. The program began in Flint, Mich., in 2024. “We know how to deliver this support efficiently and with dignity," pediatrician and Rx Kids director Mona Hanna told Science News.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Extra financial support during pregnancy and after birth can help more babies thrive in their earliest days.

The Rx Kids program in Flint, Mich., launched in January 2024, provides extra cash to pregnant residents and their infants, unconditionally. Researchers compared neonatal deaths — those in the first four weeks of life — in 2025 with those in 2021 through 2024 in Flint. The city’s neonatal mortality rate dropped from 10 deaths per 1,000 live births to 5 deaths per 1,000 live births, researchers report November 2 in JAMA Pediatrics. The early neonatal mortality rate, covering deaths in the first week of life, fell from 8 per 1,000 to 2. For the rest of Michigan, rates were stable over the study’s time period.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“As a pediatrician, there is no outcome more important than babies surviving,” says Mona Hanna of the Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in Flint, who is also the founder and director of Rx Kids. “These early findings suggest that something as simple as providing families with financial support during pregnancy and infancy may help save babies’ lives.”

Income tends to drop and expenses rise in the months before and after a birth, making the perinatal period especially difficult financially for many families. Economic precarity can expose moms and babies to health harms. For example, housing instability and homelessness is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.

Backed by public and private funds, Rx Kids got started in Flint, a city with a high rate of child poverty that has been dealing with the public health fallout of lead contamination in the water distribution system. Nearly 100 percent of the community participates in the program. Flint families receive $1,500 once during pregnancy and $500 per month in the baby’s first year. Anyone who is a resident, at least 16 weeks pregnant or with a newborn up to six months old can enroll. Families have put the extra cash toward diapers, transportation, housing and safe places for their babies to sleep, Hanna says.

“Every day, we hear from moms who tell us, ‘I can breathe’ or ‘A weight has been lifted off my shoulders.’ They tell us they feel less stressed, more hopeful, more supported and more loved,” Hanna says.

The support has had a measurable health impact, with studies linking the program to more access to prenatal care, a decrease in the preterm birth rate and in low-weight births and fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.

Rx Kids has now expanded to dozens of communities in Michigan and Ohio.

#6341. Vaping may disrupt the lung’s protective barrier after just one day

Experiments in human lung cells and hamsters suggest brief vaping exposure can disrupt protective barriers and leave lingering signs of cellular stress.

Vaping can seem easy on the lungs. New research suggests that even brief exposure can disrupt the cells that help them function.

Deep in the lung, where oxygen crosses into the blood, a single day of e-cigarette vapor was enough to injure the cells that line the smallest airways and blood vessels.

In hamsters exposed for five days, signs of cellular stress remained 10 days after exposure ended.

A separate experiment found changes in how previously exposed animals responded to a respiratory virus.

The work was done in human lung cells and tissue and in hamsters, not in people who vape. Irina Petrache, a lung specialist at National Jewish Health in Denver, was the senior author.

She is chief of the hospital’s Division of Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep Medicine, and researchers at the University of Colorado and Colorado State University took part.

“Our findings suggest that even short-term vaping exposure can initiate injury in the deepest and most delicate regions of the lung,” Petrache said.

“Importantly, some effects persisted after exposure ended and altered the immune response to a subsequent viral infection.”

The deep lung works because two thin sheets of cells stay sealed. One lines the smallest airways, and the other lines the tiny blood vessels wrapped around the air sacs.

Together, these layers allow oxygen to reach the blood while helping keep fluid out of the air spaces.

Petrache’s team worked with human cells of both kinds, some of them grown from donated lungs. They also used thin slices of lung from donors who had never smoked and had no lung disease.

The vapor came from a commercial product, JUUL pods in the Virginia Tobacco flavor with 5% nicotine. A machine puffed on the pods for three seconds every 30 seconds.

The researchers tested the vapor, the liquid, and the condensed aerosol at doses meant to mimic casual vaping.

Within a day, the cell sheets had begun to leak. The more vapor a sheet got, the more it leaked, and the highest dose did the most lasting damage.

A stressed cell runs a recycling program, breaking down its damaged parts and reusing the pieces.

Biologists call it autophagy, and it normally helps a cell survive and repair itself.

Vapor switched that program on, but the cells didn’t finish the job. Half-processed material piled up inside them. Their growth slowed, and some of the cells died.

The team traced the trouble to a stress signal inside the cell known as JNK.

When they gave the cells a drug that blocks JNK before the vapor arrived, the sheets held together better and the cleanup went further.

To examine whether the effects persisted in a living lung, the team turned to golden Syrian hamsters, whose small airways and responses to respiratory viruses resemble ours.

Six animals per group, male and female, breathed a mist made from the condensed vapor once a day for five days. Then they breathed clean air for 10 days.

By the end, the hamsters looked fine. They had not lost weight or shown signs of illness. Under the microscope, their lungs had no inflammation or scarring.

Inside the deep lung, the changes had not cleared. The marker of unfinished cleanup had risen about fourfold, and cells lining the small blood vessels carried broken strands of DNA.

About 200 genes were more active than in unexposed animals and about 300 were less active.

Some of the less active genes were associated with Th1 immunity, a branch of the immune system that helps fight viruses.

The authors wrote that many of those gene changes passed a loose statistical test but not a strict one, partly because each group held so few animals.

In 2019, an outbreak of severe lung injury hit people who used e-cigarettes, and the CDC counted more than 2,800 people hospitalized or dead from it.

A respiratory infection on top of the vaping was one suspected trigger. That outbreak is one reason the team tested what prior vaping does to an infected lung.

So a separate set of hamsters breathed the vapor mist for five days. Three days after the last dose, they received SARS-CoV-2 through the nose.

Some also received influenza A virus between the final vapor exposure and the SARS-CoV-2 infection.

In the first three days of infection, the exposed hamsters carried more SARS-CoV-2 in upper airway swabs than the unexposed ones.

A week in, their lungs showed less activity in antiviral genes and more in genes tied to breaking down and rebuilding lung tissue.

Sex made a difference. Exposed females lost more weight after infection than unexposed females, while exposed males lost less.

The inflammation and injury in the lung tissue itself showed no clear difference between the two groups.

None of this was measured in a person. Human cells in a dish and hamsters in a chamber can show what vapor does to tissue.

Studies of people who vape would need to establish whether similar changes occur in their lungs.

The team used one product in one flavor, and the hamsters breathed a condensate rather than fresh aerosol, a choice forced by biosafety rules at the time.

A condensate lacks the short-lived compounds in a fresh puff. The team also did not separate what nicotine did from what the flavoring or the other ingredients did.

Long-term lung diseases such as COPD, which narrows the airways, and fibrosis, which scars the lung, involve the same kind of leaky barrier.

The study cannot establish whether these early changes lead to chronic lung disease.

Future research could test whether blocking JNK limits the injury and whether similar changes occur in people who vape.

The full study was published in the journal JCI Insight.
